#6464. NASA Warns a Monster El Niño Could Surpass the Historic 1997 Event

An El Niño that could beat 1997’s record is taking shape in the Pacific, leaving scientists watching for its next move.

El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that returns roughly every two to seven years. Its most recent very strong events, in 1997–98 and 2015–16, disrupted weather worldwide. Consequences included fires in Indonesia and the Amazon, crop failures caused by drought in southern Africa, and heavy rain and coastal flooding in Southern California.

Satellite measurements show that the current El Niño resembles the 1997–98 event, with warm water stretching across the equatorial Pacific to South America. But that oceanic resemblance does not guarantee the same weather during winter 2026–27, as the outcome also depends on how the atmosphere responds.

Every El Niño starts with a change in the tropical Pacific’s winds. Trade winds normally push warm surface water westward, leaving sea levels higher in the western Pacific than in the east. When those winds weaken, warm water begins moving back toward the central and eastern Pacific.

As warmth spreads eastward, the trade winds weaken further and sometimes reverse, allowing still more warm water to follow. This feedback loop helps El Niño intensify.

But strength alone does not determine its effects. The location of the warmest water and the atmosphere’s response also shape the outcome. “The search for the ‘typical’ El Niño is very elusive,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). “They’re all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out.”

Scientists can track that developing pattern from space because warming water expands, raising the sea surface. Across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, unusually high water therefore provides a signal of El Niño’s heat buildup.

The maps compare sea surface height anomalies on October 13, 1997 (left), and October 12, 2026 (right). JPL scientists processed measurements from TOPEX/Poseidon and Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich, respectively. Red shows higher-than-average sea levels, white indicates normal conditions, and blue marks lower levels. Seasonal effects and long-term trends have been removed to highlight El Niño and other short-term natural changes.

“What’s unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next,” Willis said. “That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger.”

Although the 2026 El Niño developed much more abruptly, by October it shared two defining features with 1997: lower sea levels in the west and higher levels in the east, with warm, elevated water reaching South America. Willis thinks that resemblance could translate into similar impacts, including the abundant rainfall seen across California and the southern United States in 1997–98.

The powerful 2015–16 event shows why the arrangement of that heat matters. A map based on Jason-2 measurements from October 12, 2015, appears alongside the 1997 and 2026 comparisons. In 2015, the exceptionally warm, high water along the equator did not reach as far against South America. That winter, rainfall effects were concentrated more over Central America and the southeastern United States, with significant flooding in Mexico.

NOAA’s October 8, 2026, El Niño outlook assigned an 83 percent chance of a strong to very strong event through the first three months of 2027. Still, its effects during winter 2026–27 and beyond remain uncertain. El Niño’s influence passes through a chaotic atmosphere, and its signal becomes harder to distinguish beyond the tropics.

“There’s always a bit of a dice roll here,” Willis said. “Just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn’t mean it will be exactly the same—it’s just our best guess at the moment.”

It is because of the mistakes made by these scientists that we, you and I, end up with the “MAIN QUESTION OF COSMOLOGY” from Wikipedia, and its main error: “How did the Universe come into being?”!??.. After all, it is obvious and likely that the emptiness of space is ETERNAL, just like its adornment; the meaning and purpose of its existence a MAN — or, more precisely, humanity as a whole!

“Scientists can track that developing pattern from space because warming water expands, raising the sea surface.”

The sea surface is moved by tides, drifting air masses with different pressures, prevailing winds, random gusts, constructive interference of waves from all over the world, and ubiquitous, local waves. Those influences, many with short temporal duration, have to be averaged to obtain an estimate of the mean surface elevation. I have never seen an estimate of the standard deviation, often used as an estimate for the uncertainty of the mean. Things like “rogue waves,” (constructive/destructive interference) are probably usually missed, despite their great height, because of their short duration and narrow width.

Why the preference for altimetry instead of a direct measure of temperature? Because of surface mixing and the thermal inertia of water, it would seem to me that thermal IR would be a more direct measurement of the influence of El Niño on weather.

Once again, it appears necessary to remind these authors, and others, that “could” is a qualitative, not quantitative, word used to describe a low-probability event that is not, however, impossible. That is, it is permissive, not obligatory. In fact, the way it is commonly used, it has less probability of occurring than not occurring. Given that it is not associated with a numeric probability, there isn’t much else about it that can be said that is actionable. It is a word best used by a defense attorney trying to convince a jury that it is possible that his/her client is innocent of the charges brought. Our jurisprudence system is purposely designed to minimize wrongful convictions. It is embodied in the guiding principle that it is better that 10 guilty criminals are set free rather than one innocent person be punished. Science is not supposed to have such biases.

If this developing El Niño turns out to not be as strong or long-lasting as it ‘could’ be, will we hear any more about it after the fact? Will we get an explanation for why it didn’t live up to the arm waving? Probably not, because meteorologists don’t really know what triggers an El Niño. About the best they can do is predict that they will occur episodically every two to seven years. They are like a great earthquake or volcanic eruption in that respect.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6462. The Best Espresso Machines for Every Budget, Tested and Approved by a Barista

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Few things make a workday better than a delicious espresso drink, especially one made in the convenience of your own home. They’re more potent than your standard cup of coffee and require a bit more know-how, but the payoff is worth it.

Once you dip your toe into the world of espresso makers, you might find yourself overwhelmed by the dizzying array of options. Stovetop espresso makers, manual espresso machines, Nespresso, and fully automatic — there are many appliances to choose from.

To determine which is right for you, it’s helpful to start with the basics. We spoke with Stephen Welch, who has over nine years of experience in the coffee industry and serves as the coffee development manager for Pret A Manger USA. Welch is also a certified Q Grader, which is akin to becoming a sommelier in the coffee world.

To recommend the espresso machines below, we combined our own testing with thorough research. We brewed espresso with some models on this list for three months, and considered our previous experience with capsule machines and stovetop makers. Reviews from expert sites, including Good Housekeeping and coffee specialty sites like Coffee Geek, also informed our selections. We also consulted Sarah Connor, Popular Mechanics Reviews Editor and former barista, who recently did hands-on testing with two different machines in our office.

For each model, we evaluated its type, price, durability, and features, such as a built-in descaling alert, so you know when to perform a deep clean on your machine. Our list of the 10 best espresso machines includes a variety of options at different price points and for all levels of coffee-making experience.

Earlier this year, we tested this machine hands-on against a comparable De'Longhi model, and the coffee from this machine came out on top. The Breville Barista Express Impress  features an integrated conical-burr grinder with 25 grind settings, feeding directly into its impress system, which handles dosing and tamping with an assisted tamp that applies about 10kg of pressure and finishes with a 7-degree “barista twist.”

The thermo-coil heating system ensures highly accurate brew temperatures and consistent extraction. With a 250-gram bean hopper and 2-liter water reservoir, plus full stainless construction and a manual micro-foam steam wand for milk-based drinks, it delivers café-style performance in a compact home footprint.

Like a great prosumer digital camera, the Barista Express has all the capabilities and controls of a manual, pro-level espresso maker, but in a convenient package that allows even first-timers to pull a near-perfect shot. It's included grinder has controls for the amount and size of the grind, and the espresso machine gives you full control over the length of the pour. The single-boiler maker heats up in three seconds, and pulling a shot takes less than 20 seconds from grind to that first sip of frothy crema. After months of testing several machines, this one offers the most capabilities, most consistent pours, in the most user-friendly package that everyone from new enthusiasts to third-wave fanatics will appreciate.

Similar in price and capabilities to the Barista Pro, De’Longhi’s La Specialista Prestigio offers a few additional features that some espresso lovers might prefer. To take the stress out of tamping, De’Longhi has equipped this machine with a lever on the side, which you can pull to tamp your beans before removing them from the built-in grinder. That saves time, eliminates spilled grinds, and provides an even tamp. It’s the most convenient system we’ve tested, but you do lose some precision in the process, which might bother some purists.

The machine offers three heat settings for more control, however, a feature that the Barista Pro does not. It also has a secondary heating system, enabling you to move from pouring shots to steaming milk in seconds. It’s an excellent semi-automatic machine that trades some control for extra convenience while still delivering tasty shots with frothy crema.

This machine from KitchenAid delivers a professional-grade brew in a home environment. With a 2.2-liter removable water tank and durable metal-clad housing, it integrates a built-in bean hopper and grinder featuring “smart dosing” for consistent extraction. The single-spout delivery system supports 15 preset recipes (espresso, latte, Americano, etc.), and the automatic milk frother draws from a milk hose to one-touch froth and heat.

Simple, compact and affordable, the ECP36300 is capable of producing nice-tasting shots of espresso and frothy steamed milk without much fuss. The stainless steel boiler is durable, but takes longer to heat up than more expensive units. And because there’s just one heating element, you’ll need to budget even more time to fire up the steaming wand to froth your milk. The included tamper is made of flimsy plastic that can pack your grind unevenly; we suggest buying one made of metal for better results. You’ll also need your own grinder for this machine. But as long as you can summon some extra patience in the morning (a hard task, we know), this machine is great value and a good option for anyone with limited counter space.

This semi-automatic espresso maker isn’t cheap, but because it’s a KitchenAid, you know it’s extremely durable. If you’ve got a house full of regular coffee drinkers, we recommend you go with something like a KitchenAid that can stand up to heavy use. This one comes with a lot of nice features, too, like a cup warmer on top and a milk frothing attachment (sold separately). The milk frother also gets high marks from reviewers.

If you’ve got a limited budget, consider this classic stovetop espresso maker. It looks sleek on the countertop and makes a great cup of espresso without the extra cost of a larger machine. It’s not as easy to use as a fully automated machine, and it requires cleaning after each use. Because there’s no programming in the machine, it also won’t remind you about regular descaling.

The Flair allows you to customize everything about your espresso-making experience, including the water pressure, the water-to-coffee ratio, and the amount of crema or espresso foam on top. If you’re a true coffee geek, this is absolutely the machine for you. And it looks pretty darn cool, too.

At one point in my life, there was nothing more horrifying than the idea of making coffee from a single-use capsule. But after a few stays at hotels with in-room capsule espresso machines, I had to admit that the resulting espresso isn’t just good enough but actually pretty darn great. The Vertuo Next has a more plastic look than I’d like in a machine, but there is no denying how simple and dependable it is. And in terms of the environmental impact, it’s actually not as bad as you might think, particularly if you’re recycling the capsules.—J.S.

The Maestro is a beautiful machine. Of course, it should be for $1,300. But you do get a lot for the price, as you can customize just about everything such as the grind of the bean, the strength or “dose” of the coffee, and the particular type of espresso drink including a cappuccino or a flat white.

An espresso refers to how you prepare a drink rather than the type of coffee bean you use or its roast. Essentially, espresso is concentrated coffee “generally prepared quickly under pressure,” Welch says. The process involves pulling water through the cake, or bed, of packed ground coffee to extract a shot of coffee into your glass.

Water temperature and pressure are critical. According to a Smithsonian article about the history of espresso machines, Italian coffee chain Illy specifies water should be between 190 to 200 degrees Fahrenheit and under 9 atmospheres of pressure or more. These amounts vary slightly depending on equipment and the barista’s preference.

The difference between manual and automatic espresso machines also comes down to technique. Machines that “require physical force to press the water through the bed” of coffee are classified as manual, Welch says. Generally, you pull a lever, but some portable machines operate via a button or press. Manual extraction allows you to vary the pressure as you extract, which many home espresso enthusiasts want to control themselves to achieve their perfect drink. Keep in mind that manual espresso makers can have automated features.

All automatic machines use an “electrical component to activate the pump to push the water through the coffee bed,” Welch says. Automating the extraction process allows you to achieve a more consistent beverage. Although you give up a degree of control and customization, you gain a consistently dependent beverage. There are different types of automated machines:

If you are a true espresso enthusiast and have the time and interest to craft espresso according to the traditional method at home, opt for a manual or semi-automatic machine. If you want a traditionally-brewed espresso without having to prepare it yourself, consider a fully automatic machine.

Stovetop espresso makers and pod-style capsule machines also make concentrated coffee drinks, but aren’t technically espresso machines. In the case of stovetop makers, these appliances use steam pressure and don’t reach the requisite amount of water pressure. Most capsule machines add more water than a true espresso, producing something more akin to an Americano, Welch says. But you can make different specialty drinks depending on what type of pod you buy.

Despite these design differences, we chose to include stovetop and capsule machines on our list. They’re an affordable, convenient alternative to true espresso machines that can still produce a delicious, concentrated coffee drink despite the lack of manual control.

#6461. Antarctica’s Melting Ice Has Triggered a Sudden Shift Deep in the Ocean

Ocean measurements show a vast Southern Hemisphere water layer growing saltier and denser, a shift that could send more heat into deep waters than climate models predict.

Every Antarctic summer, melting sea ice sends a vast pulse of fresh water into the ocean. That seasonal supply helps sustain Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW), a layer of relatively fresh seawater that spreads across much of the Southern Hemisphere’s ocean. The AAIW helps store carbon, supply oxygen, and drive global currents, redistributing heat, fresh water, and carbon around the planet.

From 1995 to 2015, summer ice melt helped maintain this layer. But from 2016 to 2024, reduced freshwater input left it saltier, denser, and deeper, abruptly reversing its long-term trends in salinity, or salt content, and density.

The findings, published in Nature Climate Change, provide the first direct observational evidence of this change in the AAIW’s properties. The international research team analyzed data from the global Argo program, a network of around 4,000 robotic floats that sample the upper oceans, alongside satellite and atmospheric datasets.

The study was led by Associate Professor Bishakhdatta Gayen, of the University of Melbourne and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), and Kaushik Mishra, a PhD student at IISc. Gayen said:

“The Antarctic region is the freshwater engine of oceans around the globe. Melting Antarctic sea ice influences circulation thousands of kilometers away. Until 2016, the seasonal summer melt was triple the Amazon River’s entire annual flow of roughly 6,600 cubic km.

“From 2016, Antarctic sea ice shrank to record lows. This abruptly choked off that critical seasonal surge, and the meltwater delivery dropped to roughly double the Amazon’s annual flow.”

Co-author Professor Alberto Naveira Garabato, of the University of Southampton in the United Kingdom, described the changes as an urgent reminder that climate change is affecting almost every part of Earth’s surface.

“As this altered, saltier and denser water mass travels north, it moves across the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. Because this water layer forms part of the upper limb of the ocean’s global ‘overturning circulation’, a sustained shift could, over years to decades, feed into the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation – the deep-ocean current system often linked to climate stability in the North Atlantic.

“It could also ultimately influence atmospheric circulation, weather, and storm tracks in the Southern Hemisphere. However, the impact can cascade globally.”

The globe shows sea ice around Antarctica month by month. The first time-series graph shows whether sea-ice area was above or below normal (the 1993-2024 mean), based on satellite observations. The bottom graph tracks the saltiness of Antarctic Intermediate Water, a layer that sinks from the surface into the ocean’s interior, using Argo float data from 2004. From 1993 to 2015, Antarctic sea ice slowly expanded (blue trend line), releasing more freshwater, making the waters beneath it fresher. After 2016, sea ice dropped sharply (red trend line), and the layer turned saltier. Less melting ice means less freshwater reaching the ocean interior. Credit: Kaushik Mishra

Changes in how water moves between the surface and deeper layers could also affect the oceans’ role as a “climate buffer,” as Gayen described it. Oceans absorb and redistribute most of the excess heat and a large share of human CO₂ emissions, storing them for decades to centuries. This slows and moderates atmospheric warming and its immediate effects.

Mishra said the abrupt reversal revealed a critical missing feedback loop.

“The ocean absorbs over 90 percent of all heat released into the environment by human activities, with most of that heat stored in the upper ocean. A weakened AAIW layer could push more excess heat deeper. That would mean existing models are underestimating deep-ocean warming and therefore miscalculating regional sea level rise and long-term ocean and land surface temperatures.”

“If the altered AAIW changes the way surface water is carried down into deeper layers, it could affect how much carbon the ocean locks away – although the magnitude and timing are uncertain,” Gayen said.

“This could be the tipping point for the Atlantic Ocean and the AAIW current, leading to larger, longer-lasting changes to the climate in the Southern Hemisphere.”

According to Gayen, the last time the AAIW switched was at the end of the last interglacial period, around 130,000 years ago, when there was very little ice in Antarctica.

“That transition took thousands of years, not two decades,” he said.

Reference: “Reversal of Antarctic Intermediate Water trends triggered by sea ice decline” by Kaushik Mishra, Bishakhdatta Gayen and Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, 28 October 2026, Nature Climate Change. DOI: 10.1038/s41558-026-02758-y

K.M. acknowledges the Prime Minister’s Research Fellowship (grant no. PMRF-0201843). B.G. acknowledges the Ministry of Earth Sciences Grant (grant no. MOES/11/2024) and the Australian Research Council Discovery Grant (grant no. DP240102823). A.C.N.G. acknowledges U.K. Research and Innovation guarantee funding for a European Research Council Advanced Grant (grant no. EP/X025136/1).

“Every Antarctic summer, melting sea ice sends a vast pulse of fresh water into the ocean.”

Inexplicably, the authors don’t mention why the melting sea ice is ‘fresh.’ Obviously, there is some snow on top of the ice. However, the main reason is that as sea water freezes, the dissolved salts are extruded from the crystal lattice of the forming ice, and cold, dense plums of concentrated brine sink into the depths. They have ignored half of the cycle and focused on the melting half, and implied that recent behavior portends a change in the long-term trend. Predictions are difficult when a system isn’t rigorously characterized and understood, which is the case with Antarctica. Antarctic shelf ice is is notoriously variable, and thus highly unpredictable. This is Chicken Little behavior of the wet feathers variety.

“That would mean existing models are underestimating deep-ocean warming and therefore miscalculating regional sea level rise and long-term ocean and land surface temperatures.”

Water is incompressible. Therefore, thermosteric expansion of the deep water by the speculated warming will be communicated to the sea level surface. Where is the evidence that this is happening?

#6460. Brick Kilns Became Cleaner and More Profitable, but Workers Saw No Benefits

Bangladesh’s brick kilns found a way to pollute less and earn more, but workers saw no measurable improvement in their pay or working conditions.

Simple adjustments to how coal is fed and bricks are stacked helped traditional kilns burn less fuel, release less pollution, and produce better bricks. Yet a companion study found no measurable improvement in wages, health, child labor, or coercive working conditions during the study period.

The findings expose a gap between improving an industry’s performance and improving life for its workforce. They also suggest that protecting workers requires measures aimed directly at their needs.

The multiyear research effort involved Nina Brooks, an assistant professor at the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability and a faculty affiliate of its Center for South Asian Studies.

Bangladesh’s rapid urban growth depends on an industry with a substantial environmental footprint. The country is the world’s fourth-largest brick producer, and roughly 8,000 traditional kilns supply more than 90% of its domestic brick consumption. Alongside carbon emissions, the kilns release fine particles known as PM2.5. Ambient air pollution causes 4.9 million premature deaths globally, with South Asia accounting for 32% of them.

Brooks began investigating brickmaking about eight years ago during her doctoral studies. She and her collaborators mapped kilns with satellite imagery and machine learning, studied regulation, and examined health effects in communities downwind. Their work revealed why restricting kiln locations alone could not solve the pollution problem.

“Bangladesh is one of the world’s most densely populated countries,” Brooks said. “It is not feasible to move brick kilns away from all schools, health facilities, and urban centers that may be harmed by the pollution.”

Instead, researchers worked with owners, managers, and workers to improve existing operations. They introduced more continuous coal feeding, brick-stacking arrangements that improved airflow, and measures to reduce heat loss. None required replacing kilns or purchasing major new equipment.

After a small pilot, the team expanded the approach to hundreds of kilns. Results published in Science showed that training and technical support reduced energy use by about 10.5% across kilns assigned to the program. Estimated emissions fell by 171 metric tons (about 188.5 US tons) of carbon dioxide and 0.45 metric tons (about 990 pounds) of PM2.5 per kiln over a firing season.

Among kilns that adopted the practices because of the program, energy use dropped about 23%, while carbon dioxide and PM2.5 emissions each fell roughly 20%. Owners spent less on fuel and produced a greater proportion of higher-quality bricks.

Adoption had increased when researchers returned the next firing season, suggesting the changes had staying power. “Because the changes are economically beneficial for owners, they had a strong incentive to continue following them,” Brooks said.

For businesses facing expensive equipment upgrades and authorities struggling to enforce environmental rules, the findings offered a practical route to cleaner production.

The researchers then examined whether those business benefits reached workers. Bangladesh’s brick industry relies on a large, mostly informal workforce whose employment can involve debt, advance payments, long hours, hazardous conditions, and restrictions on leaving. A companion study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences examined 246 kilns in the Khulna Division and included private interviews with 1,442 workers.

Seventy percent of workers reported having no personal protective equipment, and 71% lacked a formal labor contract. Forty-two percent described restrictions on movement or communication. Across the sample, roughly 20% met the U.S. Department of State’s definitions of labor trafficking. At nearly half the kilns, at least 1 in 6 workers met those definitions.

Adult workers also reported child labor at more than 70% of the kilns, with most reported cases involving children ages 14 to 17.

The intervention lowered fuel costs by 9.6% and improved brick quality by 8.1%, but researchers detected no corresponding improvement in trafficking, child labor, wages, health, or working conditions. Although changes were possible within the study period, the economic gains did not produce measurable benefits for workers.

Higher productivity is often expected to help employees through better pay or conditions. The kiln studies show why that outcome cannot be assumed when coercion and limited bargaining power shape the labor market.

“In many countries, not just Bangladesh, labor laws are hard to enforce, particularly in informal sectors. So, it’s critical to find other ways to protect workers from exploitation,” said Grant Miller, a professor of medicine at Stanford University. “Our study shows that we cannot rely on productivity gains alone to do that, at least not in the short run. Finding approaches that work beyond regulation is a central goal of our ongoing research.”

Expanding the cleaner production program revealed that kiln owners in other regions were more reluctant to adopt the changes. In districts around Dhaka, owners were considerably less likely to adopt the practices than those in Khulna. Yet participating kilns achieved comparable reductions in fuel use and emissions, Brooks said. “So, we’re seeing greater hesitation,” she said. “But once they adopt, we see the same benefits.”

Sameer Maithel, the research team’s lead technical expert, said the reasons are still being investigated. Owners operating on narrow margins may hesitate to change familiar methods while facing unpredictable coal prices, brick demand, and regulation. Differences in kiln size, land, and production practices can also make adoption easier in one location than another.

“Informal brick production in South Asia faces a lot of uncertainty: weather, energy prices, market demand, and regulation all shift unpredictably. Many kiln owners also have limited technical and managerial support, and conditions vary from region to region,” Maithel said. “All of this makes scaling up slow and complex, and it takes sustained, dedicated effort.”

The lack of improvement for workers has prompted the team to test more direct measures. During the most recent brickmaking season, researchers returned to Khulna with recommendations developed through pilot work and conversations with workers.

They recommended masks for people crushing coal, goggles and protective footwear for fire workers, and head protection for brick carriers. Other measures included sanitation and cooking facilities, shaded rest areas, clean water, heat-stress awareness, and information about child labor.

“None of the owners I interviewed objected to improving conditions for workers, though some disagreed with specific components. They saw the cost as negligible compared to what they spend running a kiln. As they put it, if workers do better work because of it, it’s worth doing,” said Mohammad Saeed Munim, a research officer in the Health Systems and Population Studies Division of the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research in Bangladesh.

Researchers had expected more resistance. Owners’ willingness to consider these changes now gives the team an opportunity to test whether targeting workers’ daily needs can deliver improvements that greater productivity alone did not.

“Reducing emissions and air pollution from informal brick kilns: Evidence from Bangladesh” by Nina Brooks, Debashish Biswas, Sameer Maithel, Grant Miller, Aprajit Mahajan, M. Rofi Uddin, Shoeb Ahmed, Moogdho Mahzab, Mahbubur Rahman and Stephen P. Luby, 8 May 2025, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.adr7394

“Productivity gains and work conditions in coercive labor markets: Experimental evidence from the Bangladesh brick sector” by Grant Miller, Debashish Biswas, Aprajit Mahajan, Kimberly Singer Babiarz, Nina Brooks, Jessie Brunner, Sania Ashraf, Jack Shane, Alvise Scarabosio, Sameer Maithel, Shoeb Ahmed, Moogdho Mahzab, Mohammad Rofi Uddin, Mahbubur Rahman and Stephen P. Luby, 16 July 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2528388123

Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused.

Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science.

I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma.

That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. I went to the party, but I texted my mom saying I should come home because I really wasn't feeling well, which was not usual for me at all. That night I asked my mom to sleep with me because I just felt terrible.

That was Saturday. By Sunday night, the only position that I could get comfortable in was my mom holding me like a baby. My mom just held me all weekend. My whole body just hurt and I started feeling like I couldn't breathe properly. That got way worse Monday morning.

We were waiting for my pediatrician to open up and my mom suggested taking a shower, saying, "Maybe that will help you feel a bit better before we go to the doctor." She had to help me take a shower because I was so weak, I couldn't stand by myself. She stepped away for a second just to grab a towel and said that when she came back, my lips were turning gray and my eyes were starting to look sunken in. She knew that something was not right so she called my dad, who was at the grocery store, and told him to just leave everything, that we need to get to the hospital.

Allen was put on life support and had to be intubated for five weeks after getting sick with flu.

Our local hospital is just a small rural hospital — everybody gets transferred out. They diagnosed me with double pneumonia and then sent me to a different hospital 30 minutes away that specialized more in kids.

My dad rode with me in the ambulance while my mom went home and grabbed a few things — she thought we'd just be there for a few days. By the time we got to the second hospital, I was in respiratory distress. They wanted to intubate me straight away but were waiting until my mom got there so she could talk to me — my dad did the best he could, but my dad didn't know how to calm me down.

I don't think the doctors even told me that they were putting me to sleep. My mom had to be the one to tell me. I remember being very scared. They put this mask on my face for the BiPAP [bilevel positive airway pressure machine, which delivers pressurized air to a patient] and I felt like that was suffocating me. It didn't feel like it was helping at all, which, I guess, at that point, it wasn't. They were just trying everything they could. I was begging them to take it off of me, crying and just saying, "one minute, just take it off for one minute."

Finally my mom tried to calm me down and she's like, "They're gonna have to put you to sleep now." I remember her telling me, "You're just gonna go to sleep for like a couple of hours and then you're gonna wake up and you're gonna feel a lot better."

My mom had to leave the room while they were doing that. As she was walking out the door, the last thing I said was "Mom" and then I put my hands in a heart shape. That was the last thing I did and the last time my mom heard my voice for five weeks.

After I was intubated, things got worse. I had to be put on life support so needed to be moved to a bigger hospital in St. Louis, Missouri. The flight team came to evaluate me and they later told me they didn't think they were ever going to get me to Saint Louis. They thought I wasn't going to make the trip. But they said my mom was begging them to help me, everyone in my family was begging them, so they did everything they could to get me on the helicopter. They worked on me for several hours — every time they tried to move me something would go wrong — but eventually they got me there.

The doctors had to call my parents to get permission to do surgery and put me on life support. My mom said that every time she heard my dad's phone ring, she thought they were calling to tell them that I didn't make it. They were told twice that it was more than likely I was going to pass than make it. They were trying to prepare my parents that I wasn't going to make it.

After getting out of hospital, it took years for Allen to recover, eventually having part of her lung removed that had been badly damaged by the virus.

I woke up five weeks later, and it was very confusing. Everybody was told if I asked what day it was, just to tell me the day of the week. When someone accidentally told me the date, I started crying because my aunt was supposed to be getting married a few weeks later and I was worried about being at her wedding. My mom wasn't there, so my dad had to calm me down and then he told me the wedding had been pushed to October so I could be there.

The second thing I was worried about was that I was supposed to take a test on the Constitution and that I'd missed it. I ended up taking it in the hospital. I was there for 93 days. I got out the very last week of school, so I got to go in on the last day of school and surprise my classmates and my teachers.

That summer, I didn't really do anything besides go to doctor's appointments. I was doing physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy — literally all my time was spent at the hospital in therapy. I'd missed three months of school, but I got to start eighth grade with all my friends, and I ended up playing basketball again. But the next several years was a lot of hard work of trying to get back to my normal.

It probably took the rest of junior high and high school to get back to how I would have been before. It was a very long process and during that time I got sick a lot, so I ended up back in the hospital several times. And it was hard going through that as a teenager — I felt like everybody else is living their normal life, and I felt like I missed out on a lot. Looking back now, I still feel like I did miss out a lot. But I think we made the best of the circumstances.

During COVID, when I was 22, I kept getting sick, and the doctors finally told me that part of my lung was so damaged from the flu it was causing infections, so they gave me an option of getting part of my lung removed. It was a major surgery, but I did it and that was probably the best decision I ever made, because it's been five years and I have not been in the hospital once.

I moved to Florida about three years ago, and I started working as a medical assistant in a pulmonary clinic. This semester I got accepted into respiratory therapy school, so for the next two years, I'm going to be in school for respiratory therapy. It's kind of a full circle moment, to come back into the medical field, because there was a point in my life where everybody was asking me, "Oh, do you want to be a doctor? Do you want to be a nurse?" And I'm like, "Absolutely not." I was still so sick that I was there all the time. I never wanted to be there.

I went to college and I got a degree in criminal justice, but I never really knew what I wanted to do. I ended up getting a job at our local hospital — that first hospital that I went to. Every time they put me in the ER I just loved being there. That job made me realize that this is what I wanted to do.

When people hear my story, they don't realize that if I don't tell the end — after the hospital until now — they don't realize that my life didn't go back to normal after. It's taken 10 years. And it's hard. Some of the other family members that we've gotten to know through Families Fighting Flu, it's difficult listening to their stories. Sometimes I feel like I have this survivor's guilt. Their stories sound exactly like mine — but their kids didn't make it.

Before I got sick I got the flu shot every year, but that year we just got busy and it got put on the back burner. Since getting sick I have always made it a priority to get the flu shot every year. I know it is not a guarantee that I will never get the flu again — but hopefully it will reduce the chances of it ever getting that bad again.

With thanks to Families Fighting Flu, a non-profit organization that promotes flu vaccination and raises awareness of the severity of the infectious disease through families that have been affected.

#6456. A Common Plastic Could Solve a Major Problem With Living on the Moon

The same plastic that keeps marathon runners warm could help future moon bases withstand extreme temperatures and years of rough treatment.

Engineers at the University of Pennsylvania have developed an insulating material by stacking hundreds of thin sheets of Mylar. In laboratory tests, the stacks combined effective insulation in a vacuum with flexibility and resistance to repeated compression, qualities that could make them useful for long-term lunar construction.

Their study, published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, calls the material hybrid layered insulating film stacks (HyLIFS). The approach addresses a persistent engineering problem: materials that resist heat flow often struggle to withstand physical damage.

“These stacks of Mylar can bend, withstand substantial compression, and maintain their insulating performance,” says senior author Igor Bargatin, an associate professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM), “potentially allowing them to be packed, transported, and survive rough treatment over many years of use.”

On the moon, insulation must protect against temperatures ranging from hundreds of degrees below zero to the boiling point of water. But surviving those extremes is only part of the job. Materials must also endure transportation, installation, maintenance, and accidental impacts.

Some leading insulators are poorly suited to that treatment. Aerogels contain mostly empty space, making them lightweight and effective at slowing heat transfer in applications from industrial pipelines to NASA’s Mars rovers. Their porous structure, however, can also leave them susceptible to mechanical damage.

Multilayer insulation, widely used in space, takes another approach: reflective sheets separated by insulating spacers reduce heat transfer by radiation. These assemblies work well thermally, but they are not built to carry substantial loads and can tear during handling.

Making an insulator stronger can compromise its thermal performance. “For lunar infrastructure, we would ideally like both,” says Bargatin. “The ideal material is both resistant to damage and to the loss of heat.”

Mylar offered the researchers an accessible starting material. Formally known as biaxially oriented polyethylene terephthalate, or BoPET, the plastic already appears in food packaging and aerospace equipment. Combined with aluminum, it reflects infrared radiation, which is how shiny emergency blankets help marathon runners retain body heat.

The team tested several film thicknesses and coated some sheets with an extremely thin layer of aluminum oxide, also called alumina, to increase stiffness. Researchers then assembled the films individually into stacks.

“At the moment, the process is very time-consuming,” says first author Danielle R. Levin, a recent Penn chemistry doctoral graduate who also earned a master’s in MEAM. “We use two pairs of tweezers and small weights to handle and stack the delicate films. Even breathing near the stack can send the layers flying.”

Once assembled, however, the films were far tougher than their delicate handling suggested. Under vacuum conditions and compression representative of a lunar habitat with indoor air at atmospheric pressure, the best stacks matched the thermal conductivity of other high-performance vacuum insulation technologies while remaining flexible.

In separate mechanical tests, the coated stacks retained their insulating performance at the highest compressive stresses the laboratory equipment could produce. Researchers repeatedly squeezed samples to approximately 20 megapascals (about 2,900 pounds per square inch), roughly equivalent to concentrating 200 pounds onto an area the size of a fingertip.

“We were concerned about the material failing under such high compressive stress,” recalls Levin. “But the stacks didn’t survive just one high-stress cycle—they survived 10 in a row.”

That durability could make the material easier to transport and reuse, as well as more forgiving once installed. “You could use these stacks to insulate a lunar habitation, but astronauts will inevitably have little accidents where they bump into them,” says Bargatin. “When we’re talking about long-term habitation on the moon, it’s really important to have tough materials that can last long enough.”

“The combination of thermal and mechanical robustness is critical for long-term use on the moon,” says Levin. “This material could open a pathway to inexpensive, durable, and reusable lunar insulation.”

The study also identified an overlooked feature of commercial Mylar that could help explain its performance: microscopic particles added to keep the plastic from sticking to itself. These “antiblocking” particles protrude slightly from the surface, separating neighboring sheets and making thin films easier to manufacture and handle.

Their industrial purpose was already understood, but their influence on heat flow through stacked films had received little attention, according to the researchers. Because conventional multilayer insulation primarily targets radiation, there had been less reason to investigate how these particles affect heat conducted directly between sheets.

The researchers built models of heat transfer across the interfaces between layers and compared their predictions with experimental measurements. The results suggest that, in a vacuum, heat passes between sheets mainly at the tiny contact points where antiblocking particles touch neighboring films.

Those contacts could become a design tool. Instead of working around whatever particles commercial Mylar happens to contain, future insulation could use carefully selected particle sizes, numbers, and distributions to regulate heat transfer.

The particles also helped explain a result that contradicted the team’s initial expectations. Thinner sheets should allow more layers to fit into a given space, creating more interfaces that impede heat transfer. The researchers therefore expected their thinnest films to provide the strongest insulation.

Instead, the thinnest films they successfully characterized performed similarly to medium-thickness films when both received an alumina coating. The team suspects that particles in the thinner films create additional contact between neighboring layers, opening more pathways for heat to flow.

“As you compress the layers, the contact landscape changes,” says Levin. “It’s not just a matter of minimizing the film thickness or the number of particles; we must also account for how the contacts change and the films deform as pressure increases.”

Improving the material will therefore require balancing film thickness, stiffness, and particle distribution. Simply making each sheet thinner may provide little benefit if the resulting contacts allow more heat through.

The current samples cover only about one square centimeter (0.16 square inches), and manually cutting and stacking them takes hours. Producing practical insulation at the scale of a meter (about 3.3 feet) will require a much faster assembly method.

The researchers see potential in manufacturing techniques such as continuously coating large rolls of Mylar. Eventually, film thickness, coatings, and particle distribution might be adjusted before the material is wound into large stacks.

Larger versions still need testing, including whether they can withstand repeated bending, bumps, and scuffs. If the laboratory results carry over to practical production, HyLIFS could provide flexible insulation for lunar habitats, spacesuits, rovers, electronics, and other equipment that must operate for years in space.

For Levin, the findings show how much remains to be discovered in familiar materials. “The simplest configuration ended up being the best one,” she says.

Reference: “Robust Layered Thermal Insulator Film Stacks for Vacuum Applications” by D. R. Levin, M. F. Campbell, G. Aldan, O. H. Omodior and I. Bargatin, 1 September 2026, ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces. DOI: 10.1021/acsami.6c09126

#6455. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

#6452. A Planet 11 Times Bigger Than Jupiter Is Challenging What We Thought About Planet Formation

New observations of the giant exoplanet Beta Pictoris b are challenging assumptions about how and where massive planets form.

New observations of Beta Pictoris b, a massive planet orbiting a young star, are challenging a method astronomers hoped could reveal where giant planets form. More precise measurements of the planet’s atmosphere have overturned an earlier result, raising doubts about whether a particular chemical signature can reliably trace a planet’s birthplace.

Located in a 23-million-year-old planetary system, Beta Pictoris b is approximately 11 times Jupiter’s mass. It orbits about 10 astronomical units (approximately 930 million miles) from its star, completing one revolution every 23 years. Earlier atmospheric measurements suggested the planet might have formed much farther away before migrating inward, but the latest evidence points to a different possibility.

Astronomers have proposed using the relative abundance of two forms of carbon monoxide (CO) to determine where giant planets formed within their original disks of gas and dust. These molecules contain different carbon isotopes, 12C and 13C, which have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Their slightly different masses can influence how they behave during chemical processes.

The method relies on the carbon monoxide snowline, the distance from a young star beyond which temperatures become cold enough for CO gas to freeze onto dust grains. Planets forming beyond this boundary may accumulate carbon monoxide ice, potentially leaving a different isotopic signature than planets that develop in warmer regions where CO remains gaseous.

Earlier observations of Beta Pictoris b using the original GRAVITY instrument produced a relatively low ratio of 12CO to 13CO. That result appeared consistent with formation beyond the snowline, followed by inward migration to the planet’s present orbit. However, the researchers cautioned that instrumental limitations could have affected the measurement.

A team led by Antonia von Stauffenberg, a doctoral student at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy (MPIA) in Heidelberg, Germany, has now revisited the planet using GRAVITY+. The upgraded instrument operates at the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI), managed by the European Southern Observatory (ESO) in Chile.

The new observations reveal a substantially higher 12CO/13CO ratio than previously reported. While 12CO produces a readily detectable signal, its less abundant counterpart, 13CO, is considerably harder to measure accurately. GRAVITY+ provides improved adaptive optics and greater observational precision, allowing researchers to better distinguish the two molecules.

“The GRAVITY+ interferometric instrument is highly stable […], making it uniquely capable of high-fidelity characterization of directly imaged exoplanets,” says co-author and MPIA scientist Jonas Sauter.

The revised ratio agrees with independent measurements reported by González Picos et al. (2026) using a different instrument. This agreement supports the new result and indicates that systematic uncertainties affected the earlier GRAVITY measurements.

The researchers also detected tentative variations in the planet’s observed brightness. These fluctuations appear to follow a period of approximately 8.7 hours, close to the planet’s rotation period.

If confirmed, the variations could arise from atmospheric clouds or chemical differences moving in and out of view as the planet rotates. However, the evidence remains statistically weak, and more sensitive observations will be necessary to establish whether the changes are real.

“The ability to accurately constrain both isotopologues and potential rotational variability using ground-based observations of a bona fide planet such as Beta Pictoris b demonstrates the exceptional data quality achieved with the updated GRAVITY+ instrument,” says von Stauffenberg.

Under the proposed formation model, the revised carbon monoxide ratio would favor an origin inside the snowline, consistent with Beta Pictoris b’s current orbital distance. Yet the measurement also closely resembles ratios observed throughout the Solar System and the interstellar medium, the gas and dust occupying the space between stars.

Similar values have been measured in most of the roughly dozen young giant planets studied using this technique. This widespread consistency suggests that differences in carbon isotope abundances across planet-forming environments may be too small to distinguish reliably, limiting the method’s usefulness for reconstructing individual planetary histories.

“It is still difficult to utilize 13CO as a formation tracer of giant planets, due to the uncertainties that still persist in the models and measurements,” explains von Stauffenberg.

Current models may be missing important details of carbon monoxide ice chemistry in planet-forming disks. Until those processes are better understood, atmospheric carbon isotope ratios alone cannot establish whether a giant planet formed in a warm, gas-rich region or farther out among frozen materials. More precise observations and additional chemical indicators will be needed to reconstruct these planets’ origins, with GRAVITY+ offering a powerful tool for investigating both their formation and atmospheric behavior.

Reference: “13CO and potential variability in β Pictoris b with GRAVITY+” by A. von Stauffenberg, J. Sauter, P. Mollière, M. Ravet, D. Trevascus, W. Brandner, A. Berdeu, M. Bonnefoy, G. Bourdarot, J.-B. Le Bouquin, G. Chauvin, F. Eisenhauer, M. Houllé, L. Kreidberg, E. Matthews, F. Millour, J. Scigliuto, J. Wang, J. W. Xuan and Y. Zhang, 9 July 2026, Astronomy & Astrophysics. DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202660275

A new study points to testosterone and proteins in the skin as reasons why males and females experience temperatures differently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's a common observation that women often prefer warmer temperatures and feel cold more easily than men do, and the same trend appears among females of other species. Now, a study offers new clues as to what drives this preference — and testosterone may play a part.

Skin carries sensors to detect heat and cold that influence each organism's decision to stay in or move out of an environment. The new study, published Oct. 28 in the Journal of Physiology, found that these sensors activate at higher temperatures in female mice, which appears to shift their preferred temperature roughly 7 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) higher than that of male mice. Testosterone seems to influence this difference in activation.

"You could say it's just a cute observation of no particular importance," said study co-author Peter McNaughton, a pharmacologist at King's College London who studies pain, thermal sensation and thermoregulation. "[But] it's got practical ramifications," in that it might be important in designing buildings and spaces that accommodate people, he told Live Science.

Proteins in the skin's nerve endings activate in response to warmth or cold. "You can look at them like little electrical generators in the nerve endings," said Dr. Michael Caterina, a neuroscientist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the research.

When activated, these proteins allow charged ions to enter sensory nerve cells, which, in turn, transmit electrical signals to the brain. The circuits a given nerve cell connects to determines our perception of heat or cold, Caterina told Live Science.

Beyond humans, it is known that many female animals, including mice and birds, prefer slightly warmer temperatures than their male counterparts do. So the researchers set up an experiment to investigate these differences.

They put 30 male and 27 female mice on two adjacent plates of different temperatures — one at 91.4 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius) and another that varied between lower and higher temperatures. A camera tracked the mice's movements and calculated how much time they spent on each plate.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both male and female mice spent more time at the 91.4 F plate when the second plate was cooler. However, when put next to a plate measuring 100.4 F (38 C), female mice spent significantly more time on the warmer plate than male mice did. The average preferred surface temperature was approximately 89.6 F (32 C) for male mice and 96.8 F (36 C) for female mice.

"Since the top of the cage was completely open, there was no question of the air temperature affecting the mice," McNaughton said, so the preference was driven solely by the sensors in their skin. The researchers also measured the internal and skin temperatures of the mice and confirmed that there were no significant differences between the sexes on those fronts.

The scientists explored what would happen if they genetically deleted the warmth-detector protein. In male mice, this reduced their avoidance of the warmer plate, suggesting this protein normally sends a signal that discourages them from staying on warmer surfaces. The mice's preferred temperature also rose to about 95 F (35 C), closer to that of females.

The study suggests that testosterone somehow tweaks the function of heat-sensing nerves in the skin.

In female mice, deleting or blocking the protein did not have any significant effect.

The team then tried eliminating or blocking the coolness-detecting protein, finding that males and females didn't avoid the cool plates as strongly as they did before. Female mice also spent less time on the warmer plates, but males' preference for the warmer plates didn't change.

"Females are a little bit more responsive to activation of the cold receptor," Caterina said, "and a little bit less responsive to activation of the warmer receptor." That's despite the temperature-sensing neurons in both sets of mice working identically, the team found.

The researchers suspected that sex hormones might help to explain this difference.

They gave a group of male mice a drug that blocks the production of testosterone. Weeks after the treatment, these mice spent more time on the 38 C plate than males with normal testosterone. Meanwhile, female mice given testosterone lost their preference for warmer temperatures.

Interestingly, giving male mice female hormones, including forms of estrogen and progesterone, did not affect their temperature preferences. And blocking the hormones in female mice also had no effect. These hormones are known to influence other aspects of temperature regulation in the body, though, such as heat dissipation through the skin; but in this case, they didn't seem to affect animals' perception of temperature.

"So it really seems as though testosterone is the most important determinant," McNaughton said. But these changes were only partial; testosterone did not completely reverse the differences between the sexes. "So there is something else going on that we weren't able to identify," he added.

The exact mechanism for how testosterone impacts the sensor proteins is not clear. Because the effect happened over weeks, researchers suggested that it did not directly affect the temperature-sensing proteins. It might instead act indirectly by influencing the activity of genes, but further studies would be needed to confirm this idea.

Although the researchers did not conduct any tests in humans, McNaughton noted that the same sensor proteins are present in people and that studies with humans suggest that they behave in a similar way.

This research provides "valuable information" for understanding how the proteins responsible for sensing temperature work, Caterina said. Understanding these mechanisms could be useful for studying conditions like neuropathic pain, in which people's sensitivity to heat and cold is enhanced.

"What kinds of signals create our daily experiences around temperature is by itself very important," he told Live Science. "It's a big part of understanding ourselves as living beings."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6447. James Webb’s Mysteriously Bright Galaxies May Finally Have an Explanation

Calculations suggest powerful ultraviolet light from young stars could sweep gas out of early galaxies while leaving dense star-forming regions intact, offering a clue to their mysterious brightness.

The James Webb Space Telescope has revealed something unexpected about the early universe: bright galaxies were far more common just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang than astronomers thought possible. A new analysis suggests these galaxies may not necessarily be producing more light than expected. Instead, powerful ultraviolet radiation from young stars could be clearing away gas and dust, allowing more of their light to reach us.

Researchers at the Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute in New York City and the University of Texas at Dallas investigated this possibility by examining how ultraviolet light called Lyman-alpha radiation interacts with material surrounding young stars. Their findings, published November 4 in The Astrophysical Journal, suggest that this radiation can drive gas and dust out of less dense regions of galaxies, potentially explaining why some of the earliest galaxies appear unusually bright.

“Our results show Lyman-alpha radiation can push low-density gas and dust away really, really fast,” says Shyam Menon, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute’s Center for Computational Astrophysics and the study’s lead author. “It can sort of clear the ‘fog,’ allowing us to see stars in the early universe much more clearly than we would otherwise.”

Lyman-alpha radiation forms when an electron collides with a hydrogen atom or joins a hydrogen ion, and it can be especially abundant in regions where young stars are forming. When this light encounters gas or dust, it transfers momentum to the material, creating pressure that can push it outward.

What makes Lyman-alpha radiation particularly powerful is how hydrogen responds to it. While most absorbed light is released at a different wavelength, hydrogen atoms almost immediately re-emit Lyman-alpha radiation at the same wavelength, allowing nearby atoms to absorb and release it repeatedly. These repeated interactions increase the force exerted by the light, potentially pushing surrounding material away from regions where stars are forming.

Astronomers have long suspected that this pressure could reshape stellar nurseries by removing gas needed for star formation, possibly even stopping the process under extreme conditions. However, the repeated interactions between radiation and hydrogen are difficult to reproduce in computer simulations, making it challenging to determine how much influence the radiation actually has.

“We’ve known for a very long time that Lyman-alpha radiation could be important because it carries a lot of force,” Menon says. “But we’ve never actually been able to estimate how important it is in a realistic environment because of how challenging it is to model.”

To address this problem, Menon and collaborator Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas analyzed snapshots from an existing simulation of a star-forming region in the early universe. Rather than tracking every interaction between light and matter, they calculated how much pressure Lyman-alpha radiation would exert on the surrounding gas and dust.

Their calculations revealed that the radiation behaves differently depending on the density of the surrounding material. In dense star-forming regions, gravity remained strong enough to hold gas and dust in place despite the outward pressure, suggesting that Lyman-alpha radiation had little effect on star formation there. In less crowded regions between stars, however, the radiation could overcome gravity and drive material outward at high speeds.

Multiple views of a 2.5-million-year simulation visualizing a gas cloud as it is cleared away and the formation of stars. From left to right, the views show the gas density, ionization, and temperature. Credit: Shyam Menon (Flatiron Institute) and Aaron Smith (UT Dallas)

“When the density is low enough, the Lyman-alpha radiation can push the gas to really high speeds, launching explosive winds that can shoot material clear out of the galaxy,” Menon says.

These winds could help explain the unexpectedly bright galaxies detected by the James Webb Space Telescope. By removing loosely distributed gas and dust from between stars, the radiation may create clearer paths for starlight to escape, making distant galaxies appear brighter without requiring them to produce unusually large amounts of light.

Important questions remain, particularly about the properties of dust in the early universe and how radiation interacts with moving gas as stars form. Researchers will need more comprehensive simulations that account for these processes together to better understand their influence on early galaxies.

Recent work by Olof Nebrin of Stockholm University and study co-author Smith has demonstrated that these interactions can be modeled in two dimensions, although more realistic three-dimensional simulations remain a challenge.

“But the hope is that in the coming years, with improvements to computing power and the development of more effective algorithms, we can eventually do these simulations in three dimensions.”

Reference: “Lyα Radiation Pressure in Dense Star Clusters: Implications for Star Formation and Winds at Cosmic Dawn” by Shyam H. Menon and Aaron Smith, 4 November 2026, The Astrophysical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/aeaed6
