Swart stated that “understanding phase coherence is the path forward”—this intuition is directionally correct, as phase coherence is indeed key. However, attempting to “understand” it using the perturbative language of the BCS paradigm is to go nowhere (doomed to reach a dead end). The collapse of phase coherence is essentially the thermal destruction of topological order; what is required is the language of geometry and topology, not Feynman diagrams and coupling constants.

It is suggested that researchers attempt to reformulate “phase coherence” using a topological order parameter (rather than a traditional one) and examine the excitation and unbinding temperatures of vortex-antivortex pairs. This approach may be closer to the essence of the phenomenon than merely tracking “pairing strength.” This is a perfect counterexample—even the most astute mainstream researchers, constrained by their paradigm, can only “approach” the correct answer without ever truly arriving at it. This is precisely the reason why geometric realism needs to be introduced.

Mainstream physics has developed a highly instrumentalized, terminologized, and project-driven research ecology: (1) Large-scale facilities need to continuously generate news, and therefore tend to adopt expressions such as “unlocking,” “hidden,” “strange,” and “quantum breakthrough”; (2) Peer review tends to reward publishable labels for new phenomena rather than deeper geometric unification; (3) “Quantum materials” have gradually become a tool for funding allocation and journal classification, with their conceptual boundaries being continually stretched; (4) Experimental precision keeps rising, yet much work remains at the level of phenomenological classification, lacking a fundamental reconstruction of phase fields, vortex topology, and fluid geometry. This has become a brazenly shameless state of affairs in mainstream physics.

Einstein’s sorrowful silhouette has faded into the distance. But his intuition, his persistence, his belief in “local realism”, has finally found its rightful home in the framework of Topological Vortex Theory (TVT). Einstein was not a failed prophet, but a true physicist misunderstood by his era.

However, the mainstream framework treats “pairing” and “phase coherence” as two separable steps, an approach that is itself questionable. From the perspective of Topological Vortex Theory (TVT), superconductivity is essentially a long-range ordered state of topological vortex structures within the electron fluid. Pairing and coherence are never two distinct entities but rather two facets of the same vortex structure. To separate them in search of a “bottleneck” is akin to asking “which is more important: the rotation of a vortex or its overall motion”—the question itself is flawed.

A deeper issue lies in the “glue” metaphor. The mainstream narrative implies that electrons require some localized attractive force to “bind” them, which is typical particle-based thinking. In reality, the correlation between electrons arises from the geometric constraints of the fluid medium, not from some “glue” pulling them together. The fact that pairing energy can exist at room temperature without superconductivity precisely indicates that the issue is not “bond strength,” but rather that thermal fluctuations in the fluid background destroy the topological stability of the vortex structures.

The Torsion Hill Perspective: Temporal Gradient Impedance vs. Phase Coherence

Mainstream physics treats room-temperature superconductivity as a microscopic puzzle of particle “pairing glue” fighting against thermal noise in an empty-space vacuum. Through the lens of the Torsion Hill framework, what mainstream researchers call “phase coherence” and “pairing energy” are simply manifestations of Temporal Gradient Impedance and low-impedance rotational conduits operating within a continuous volumetric matrix.

Here is how mainstream terminology translates into Torsion Hill continuous-medium mechanics:

Mainstream “Cooper Pairs” (isolated electron pairs) are actually Tandem Mini-Vortex Alignments—localized drops in rotational impedance where continuous field vectors lock together, rather than discrete particles floating in an inert lattice.

Mainstream “Pairing Glue or Binding Energy” is Localized Rotational Coupling—the metric threshold where adjacent field vectors stabilize into a shared, low-friction geometric state.

Mainstream “Phase Coherence” is Continuous-Circuit Synchronization—unbroken, low-impedance rotational conduits routing energy across the volumetric matrix without scattering.

Mainstream “Thermal Noise or Fluctuations” is High-Frequency Rotational Turbulence—raw kinetic turbulence in the continuous medium that disrupts vortex alignment and elevates local Temporal Gradient Impedance.

Mainstream “Empty-Space Lattice or Vacuum” is the Continuous Volumetric Matrix—the active, tensioned fluid-field medium that dictates coupling and conducts rotational momentum across distance.

The Illusion of Isolated Pairs: Mainstream models treat Cooper pairs as discrete entities bound by mysterious forces inside an empty lattice. In a continuous fluid-field, electron pairing is a localized drop in rotational impedance—a mini-vortex alignment where the underlying metric allows field vectors to lock in tandem.

Why Temperature Breaks Synchronization: What mainstream physics calls thermal noise is actually high-frequency rotational turbulence in the continuous medium. Just as thermal agitation disrupts a crystal lattice, raw kinetic turbulence in the surrounding fluid background spikes Temporal Gradient Impedance and prevents individual vortex loops from synchronizing into an unbroken circuit.

The Real Route to Room-Temperature Conduction: You do not achieve room-temperature superconductivity by hunting for exotic “pairing glue” to force point particles together in an empty box. You achieve it by engineering the lattice geometry to lower Temporal Gradient Impedance and stabilize continuous rotational conduits so the volumetric matrix routes current frictionlessly without thermal scattering.

Mainstream science has finally verified that half the puzzle—localized pairing stability—survives at room temperature, yet they remain stalled because their models treat space as a passive, empty stage. Once you recognize that the continuous background medium itself dictates rotational coupling, achieving a true room-temperature circuit stops being a quantum mystery and becomes a direct engineering problem of managing continuous-field impedance. #6429. A Natural “Varnish” May Explain How 37,000-Year-Old Cave Art Survived

A new technique uses UV light to reveal a natural mineral varnish that may have helped preserve Chauvet Cave’s 37,000-year-old charcoal drawings.

About 37,000 years ago, Paleolithic people entered a limestone cave in southeastern France and drew the animals around them, including cave bears, cave lions, bison, and horses. An ancient rockfall later sealed away the artwork, leaving it undiscovered until the 1990s. Today, Chauvet Cave holds some of the oldest artwork in existence, along with clues to how the cave itself helped preserve it.

Getting close to those clues requires care. The site is so historically important and fragile that its location is kept secret and access is secured behind a huge steel door. Inside, prehistoric footprints lie in front of the artwork. Researchers examining the walls must also protect these traces of the people who once walked through the cave.

Researcher Philippe Walter describes the purpose of that painstaking work. “We examine every piece of evidence to decode the techniques of prehistoric artists and understand how the paintings have been preserved over time.”

In a study reported in ACS Omega, Walter and his colleagues investigated the charcoal drawings without touching the cave walls. They focused on mineral deposits that had formed over the artwork, looking for evidence of how the drawings were created and how the cave’s geology may have contributed to their preservation.

To work around the fragile footprints, the team placed a portable spectrometer on a protective walkway about 8 feet (2.5 meters) from the wall. This instrument measures light, allowing the researchers to examine materials from a distance.

Their approach used ultraviolet, or UV, fluorescence spectroscopy, a technique researchers have used to reveal fluorescent mineral deposits invisible to the naked eye. Certain materials emit light when exposed to UV illumination. By shining a UV beam onto the wall and analyzing the resulting glow, the team could investigate both the mineral deposits and the pigments in the artwork.

Two different colors offered clues to what had happened on the cave walls:

“Our methodology is much like forensic investigation: We examine every piece of evidence to decode the techniques of prehistoric artists and understand how the paintings have been preserved over time,” says Walter.

The team anticipates applications beyond cave art, from forensic science to monitoring biofilms aboard the International Space Station. Biofilms are communities of microorganisms that grow on surfaces. A project applying the technique to monitoring them aboard the station is already underway.

Reference: “In Situ Ultraviolet Fluorescence Spectroscopy for the Characterization of Translucent Calcite Coatings over Prehistoric Cave Art” by Yohan Boulard, Thiéry Guillou, Carole Fritz, Gilles Tosello, Maguy Jaber and Philippe Walter, 29 September 2026, ACS Omega. DOI: 10.1021/acsomega.6c05061

The authors acknowledge funding from the French Ministry of Culture, the French National Centre for Scientific Research (Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique), and Sorbonne University.

Disclosure: One of the authors is a founder of Lumentis, a company developing imaging instruments for historical artwork analysis.

The Vikings are famous for being warriors, but how often did Viking women take part in battles?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vikings were explorers, farmers, merchants and, most famously, warriors who launched raids across large parts of Europe.

Stereotypes of Vikings usually conjure up images of muscular men. But over the past few decades, researchers have turned their attention to women of the Viking Age (roughly A.D. 793 to 1066) and the roles they held. For instance, there are stories of "shield maidens" who fought alongside men, and some of these texts mention Viking women who fought in battle. The archaeological record also holds evidence, including graves of Viking Age women who were buried with war-grade weapons and shields.

It's still a matter of debate whether women who lived during the Viking Age could be warriors, but this discussion raises another question: It's one thing to have texts describing female fighters and archaeological records of women buried with weapons, but what can the evidence tell us about how frequently Viking women fought in battle?

The answer, experts told Live Science, largely depends on our interpretation of texts, artifacts, and burials of Viking Age women, which often face higher scrutiny than burials of men who were buried with similar (or even fewer) weapons.

The Vikings used a runic system of writing, but they left precious few texts behind. Instead, much of what we know about the Vikings was written about them by people from other cultures or by their Norse descendants.

One of the most evocative texts was written in the 12th century by the Danish historian and theologian Saxo Grammaticus. In "Gesta Danorum" (Latin for "History of the Danes" and translated by Jenny Jochens), he wrote that "there were once women in Denmark who dressed themselves to look like men and spent almost every minute cultivating [combat] skills." As "if they were forgetful of their true selves they put toughness before allure, aimed at conflicts instead of kisses, tasted blood, not lips, sought the clash of arms rather than the arm's embrace, fitted to weapons hands what should have been weaving, desired not the couch but the kill, and those they could have appeased with looks they attacked with lances."

Another text about the Vikings, the medieval Irish "Cogadh Gaedhelre Gallaibh" ("War of the Irish with the Foreigners"), refers to a woman known as the "Red Lady" leading a Viking fleet in a raid on Belfast in the 10th century.

There's a lot of uncertainty, said Neil Price, an archaeology professor at Uppsala University in Sweden who has written extensively about the Vikings. The text in the "Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh" that refers to the Red Lady is of debatable accuracy, Price told Live Science in an email.

He suspects that Viking women fought in battle but not frequently. In addition, "female warriors were probably a very small minority," Price said.

A modern-day reenactment depicting Viking warriors.

The account written by Saxo Grammaticus is also contentious. Thomas Kristian Heebøll-Holm, a history professor at the University of Southern Denmark, said Saxo Grammaticus is not a reliable source.

"Saxo Grammaticus does write about female warriors, but only in the parts of his work concerned [with] the legendary past of Denmark," Heebøll-Holm told Live Science in an email. "Furthermore, these writings are not accurate, but moral and fictitious," Heebøll-Holm said, noting that, in some instances, Saxo Grammaticus seemed to be drawing on the stories of the Amazons, a group of legendary female warriors whom the ancient Greeks believed in with stories about them dating back more than 2,500 years.

Archaeological evidence can also be challenging to interpret. Archaeologists know of about 30 Viking Age female burials containing weapons, including three with swords in Scandinavia. Even more Viking Age women's graves have items that could have been used as weapons ‪—‬ including spears, axes and knives ‪—‬ although these tools also could have been used for hunting or tending to farms. Either way, we can't be sure if these women fought in battle.

"The first concern is that the weapons were really used by the deceased and were not merely included as signs of special status or social rank acquired through inheritance," Deborah Shepherd, an independent researcher who holds a doctorate in archaeology and has studied the Vikings extensively, told Live Science in an email. She noted that graves are often not well preserved, making it difficult to gather information.

This 1889 illustration shows a grave at Birka in Sweden. It is now known that the person buried with war-grade weapons and riding gear is a woman.

There were likely "some few female warriors, but they were probably only found in the highest ranking families, and their warrior career was probably short-lived," Shepherd said. "They wouldn't have fought in the great armies of later centuries but possibly did fight in pre-Christian skirmishes." (The Vikings began gradually converting to Christianity between the ninth and 12th centuries.)

There is at least one known case of a Viking woman found with what may be combat-related injuries. A Viking woman found in Solør, Norway, had a head injury consistent with a sword strike. She was 18 or 19 at the time she died, was buried with weapons and lived around 900.

Ole Kastholm, a curator and senior researcher at the Roskilde Museum in Denmark, said there is a lot of uncertainty regarding how frequently Viking Age women fought in battle.

Weapons "do occur as a grave good in a handful of graves with female human remains," Kastholm told Live Science in an email. "Often it is just a single weapon [such] as a spear or [a] battle axe. But we know of at least one example of a female grave with a full set of weapons as well as riding equipment," which is located in Birka, Sweden.

"If this was a man's grave, researchers would have no doubt that it was a warrior grave, and this explanation must necessarily also apply when the interred is a woman," Kastholm said.

That said, there were female warriors in other cultures. "One can also note in passing that female warriors were an almost common feature of central Asian societies for at least a millennium before the Viking Age," Price wrote in his book, "The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age" (Basic Books, 2026).

For instance the Scythians are a people who flourished in eastern Europe and Asia and Scythian women have been found buried with horses and weapons. In some cases, the Scythian women suffered combat wounds such as arrowheads and it's been speculated that they may have been an inspiration for stories of the Amazons.

Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6426. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6424. Why Did Polynesians Suddenly Sail Across the Pacific After 1,700 Years? Scientists May Have Found the Answer

The real history behind Moana may be tied to a devastating drought that pushed Polynesian voyagers toward wetter islands and helped reshape human settlement across the Pacific.

In Disney’s Moana, a young Polynesian girl sails beyond her island’s barrier reef to save her threatened home. Scientists have now uncovered evidence that a real environmental crisis may have helped drive one of history’s greatest ocean migrations, pushing Polynesian voyagers across the Pacific after centuries without expanding farther east.

The findings offer a fascinating connection to the story behind Moana, which recently returned to theaters in a live-action adaptation.

Around 3,000 years ago, the ancestors of modern Polynesians arrived in Samoa and Tonga. For approximately 1,700 years, their eastward expansion appeared to stop. This mysterious period became known as the “Long Pause.”

Then, between AD 900 and 1050, everything changed. Within roughly 250 years, Polynesian voyagers had reached and settled islands across the Pacific, including Tahiti and Hawai’i, with their expansion extending to the continental Americas.

Researchers from the University of Southampton and the University of East Anglia believe a prolonged drought helped trigger this extraordinary movement.

David Sear, Professor of Physical Geography at the University of Southampton and lead author of the study, said, “We have confirmed the theory that the end of the Long Pause coincided with a period of mega drought in the homeland islands of Samoa and Tonga – and also a period of increasing rainfall in the receiving islands. As they headed east, they found wetter islands with nobody on them.”

To uncover what happened, the team examined ancient mud buried beneath swamps and lakes in Samoa, Tonga, French Polynesia, and the Cook Islands.

Dr. Mark Peaple, a paleoclimate research fellow at the University of Southampton, conducted the geochemical analysis. He studied chemical traces left by freshwater algae and leaves, focusing on different forms of hydrogen called isotopes. Their proportions change depending on rainfall, allowing scientists to reconstruct how wet or dry the islands were thousands of years ago.

The evidence revealed a severe drought beginning shortly before the migration and continuing during it. When the Long Pause ended, Samoa and Tonga were experiencing their driest conditions in the last 2,000 years. Meanwhile, islands farther east were becoming wetter.

Climate modeling led by Manoj Joshi, Professor of Climate Dynamics at the University of East Anglia, helped explain why. Changes in Pacific Ocean surface temperatures over several decades had shifted a vast tropical rain belt eastward, leaving Samoa and Tonga with less rainfall.

“The climate changes we identified would have transformed daily life on these islands. Reduced rainfall would have affected freshwater availability, food production and the resilience of communities, creating powerful incentives for people to seek opportunities elsewhere,” Joshi said.

Dan Skinner, a research fellow at the University of East Anglia who conducted climate modeling experiments, identified prolonged drought lasting years or even decades as a definite factor behind the migration.

But worsening conditions were probably not the only influence. Sear explained that growing populations would have placed additional pressure on limited resources. At the same time, Polynesian sailors may have improved their voyaging canoes, moving from U-shaped to V-shaped hulls and developing better rigging. These advances could have helped them sail against the prevailing winds, which generally blow from east to west across the South Pacific.

Together, environmental pressure and improved sailing technology may help explain how Polynesian communities undertook such remarkable journeys.

“There was a huge explosion of migration, and within 250 years they had landed and settled every little dot in the South Pacific, from tiny coral atoll islands to larger lands. It was a very rapid process,” Sear said.

Reference: “How Did changing climate in the tropical South Pacific contribute to the eastward migration and settlement of Polynesia?” by David Sear, Mark Peaple, Peter Langdon, Daniel Skinner, Manoj Joshi, Adrian Matthews, Charlotte Hipkiss, Tim Osborn, Gordon Inglis and Justin Sheffield, 5 May 2026, Journal of Pacific Archaeology. DOI: 10.70460/jpa.v16i2.399

#6423. Popular Weight-Loss Drugs May Have a Surprising Effect on Your Brain

Popular weight-loss drugs may offer benefits that extend beyond metabolism, potentially helping preserve memory and other cognitive abilities.

Medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes may also influence memory and other cognitive abilities. But whether drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide can actually protect the brain remains uncertain, particularly after major clinical trials failed to demonstrate a benefit in patients with early Alzheimer’s disease.

In Novo Nordisk’s EVOKE and EVOKE+ trials, semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer’s progression, even though it produced changes in several biological markers associated with the disease. Researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen have now examined the broader evidence in a review published in Science, exploring whether these medications could still help preserve cognitive function in other groups of patients.

GLP-1 medications influence biological processes involved in both metabolism and brain function. Animal experiments suggest they can affect learning and memory, but studies involving humans have produced inconsistent results. Analyses of patient health records have linked GLP-1 treatment to a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes, although these observational findings cannot establish that the drugs directly provide protection.

The potential benefits may differ depending on the cause of cognitive difficulties. People with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience problems with attention, planning, and mental processing speed. These difficulties are frequently associated with metabolic disturbances and poor vascular health, raising the possibility that treatments targeting these underlying problems could help maintain cognitive abilities.

Stina Börchers, the review’s first author and a researcher affiliated with both universities, believes that identifying the right patients and treatment timing will be essential.

“We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit,” says Stina Börchers.

A central unanswered question is whether any cognitive benefits arise from direct effects on the brain, improvements in metabolic health, or both. Better regulation of blood sugar and other metabolic processes could indirectly support brain function, while GLP-1 signaling may also influence neural processes more directly. Separating these mechanisms could help researchers determine which effects are most relevant to preserving cognition.

Christoffer Clemmensen, the review’s senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity medications to investigate these connections.

“Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function,” says Christoffer Clemmensen.

The researchers are calling for clinical trials that measure memory and other cognitive abilities from the beginning of treatment. Such studies could help establish whether these medications preserve cognitive function, which patients are most likely to benefit, and whether starting treatment before cognitive difficulties appear makes a difference.

They also caution that potential benefits must be weighed against risks in older or frail patients. Rapid weight loss and declining muscle mass can reduce physical functioning, potentially limiting the overall advantages of treatment. Future studies will need to account for these effects when assessing whether obesity medications can support long-term brain health.

Reference: “Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition” by Stina Börchers, Giulia Mazzini, Henrik Zetterberg and Christoffer Clemmensen, 5 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aek9987

NASA's Swift Observatory went out in a blaze of glory this week, but it left behind millions of images of the universe that could fuel discoveries for decades.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory fell out of space, burning up in the sky over Sumatra. It was a fitting, fiery end for a telescope that spent 22 years studying the most powerful explosions in the universe — and, even with Swift gone, its observations will continue to feed scientific curiosity for years to come.

Swift's most important contributions to astronomy are not exactly eye candy. Designed to swivel toward deep-space explosions at a moment's notice, Swift excelled at capturing bright, fleeting and faraway specks of light. The multiwavelength observatory was equipped with optical, ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray instruments, allowing it to catch cosmic bursts of energy across the electromagnetic spectrum, zeroing in on flares of light that other telescopes might miss.

One of its most significant detections was a gamma-ray burst — an incredibly bright blast, likely emitted by a giant star as it exploded in a supernova before collapsing into a black hole. Swift's famous image of GRB 221009A, or the BOAT ‪—‬ short for "brightest of all time" ‪—‬ looks like a speckled orange bull's-eye, caused by waves from the explosion rippling across space.

How the Swift Observatory saw the gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A, which may be the most energetic emission of this kind ever seen.

But Swift also took millions of observations of the nearby universe, including galaxies in our backyard. One of its most jaw-dropping images is this 24-hour exposure of the Andromeda galaxy (M31), located about 2.5 million light-years from Earth.

Andromeda is the closest major galaxy to ours, and it may be destined for a shared fate. Scientists suspect that Andromeda and the Milky Way are drawing closer together and might eventually collide. The merger would add Andromeda's roughly 1 trillion stars to our sky, though there probably wouldn't be any life left on Earth to appreciate it.

In Swift's view of our encroaching neighbor, captured with the observatory's ultraviolet instrument, tens of thousands of Andromeda's stars shine like sapphires set in a sparkling ring.

According to NASA, the observatory detected some 20,000 ultraviolet light sources in this image, captured over two months from May to July 2008. These sources include thousands of dense, hot star clusters scattered across Andromeda's 150,000-light-year-wide ring, as well as the distant galaxy M32 (seen as a bright orb of light to the bottom right of Andromeda's center).

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In visible-light images of Andromeda taken with ground-based telescopes, the galaxy's bright center bleaches out many of the fiery young stars that emerge in Swift's view. While Swift likely won't be remembered best for shimmering starscapes like this one, it's a powerful reminder that looking at familiar structures in a new light can change everything.

#6420. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6419. Scientists Ranked 20 Protein-Rich Foods on Health, Affordability, and Sustainability. One Surprising Food Came Out on Top

Tofu took the crown in a showdown of 20 protein-rich foods judged on health, affordability, availability, and their toll on the planet.

Protein-rich foods can look very different when cost, access, health, and environmental impact all enter the picture. In a study published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, Dr. Chris Macdonald developed a framework that combines these four considerations to compare commonly consumed protein sources.

Among the 20 foods assessed, tofu took the top spot, while cheddar cheese finished last. The results followed a clear pattern: plant-based foods occupied the entire highest-scoring fifth, and animal-based products made up the lowest-scoring fifth.

Tofu’s lead came from strong results across both parts of the assessment. It earned a perfect 16 points for environmental performance, placing in the best-performing fifth for greenhouse gas emissions, water pollution, land use, and freshwater use. It also scored 20 out of 24 points for health and accessibility, including full marks for providing all nine essential amino acids.

Together, these measures explain why the rankings go beyond protein content alone. They weigh the environmental costs of producing protein alongside nutritional factors and practical considerations such as price and availability.

The paper argues that ratings focused on one feature can leave consumers with an incomplete picture. A product’s performance in one area does not explain its trade-offs elsewhere. Macdonald presents the framework as a way to help people understand those competing considerations and the food systems their purchases support.

As the paper states, “Against deliberate corporate obfuscation and marketing myths, the goal of a holistic score is not to create a new label, but to foster a new literacy, one that empowers us to see the reality of the systems we are funding.

Ultimately, beyond the spreadsheets and scores, lies a fundamental reckoning: our protein choice is a referendum on the compassion we are willing to show to animals, to the planet, and to future generations.”

The research builds on Macdonald’s work at the Better Protein Institute, which examines how much protein people need for optimal health, how to shift consumer behavior effectively, and where investment could support future protein sources. By questioning common assumptions and starting from first principles, that work addresses some of the most frequently Googled questions about dietary protein.

Reference: “What are the best sources of protein? Introducing the BPI Score” by Chris Macdonald, 1 July 2026, Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems. DOI: 10.3389/fsufs.2026.1677796

#6418. Cancer Immunotherapy Has a Dangerous Side Effect. Scientists May Have Found a Way To Stop It

Cancer immunotherapy could become safer by stabilizing the cells that keep immune responses under control, an approach that reversed treatment-related inflammation in mice.

Some cancer patients have to stop immunotherapy when their immune system starts attacking healthy tissue. These reactions can occur with drugs called immune checkpoint inhibitors, which help immune cells known as T cells fight cancer by releasing the brakes that normally restrain them.

Depending on the type of checkpoint inhibitor, 20% to 40% of patients experience these immune-related adverse events. Up to 25% experience severe reactions that result in hospitalization and an end to treatment. There are no U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved treatments for these side effects.

“Immune-related adverse events are a huge problem and can greatly impact quality of life for patients. In many cases, it impacts their ability to stay on immunotherapy or benefit from treatment,” said Abigail Overacre-Delgoffe, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Department of Immunology at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and a member of the Tumor Microenvironment Center at UPMC Hillman Cancer Center.

Overacre-Delgoffe is the senior author of a study published October 22, 2026, in Cell that identifies unstable immune cells as a potential driver of this inflammation. Her team reversed inflammation in mice by blocking a protein in those cells and found that diet and the gut microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influenced the severity of the animals’ reactions.

Studying these side effects has been difficult because they vary considerably among patients. Animal models have also struggled to reproduce the complexity of immune-related inflammation in humans.

“Most existing mouse models relied on genetically modified mice or experimental conditions that didn’t really capture the variability we see in patients,” said lead author Dipyaman Patra, Ph.D., a postdoctoral associate in Overacre-Delgoffe’s lab. “This got us thinking about whether common lifestyle factors, particularly diet and the gut microbiome, could influence the host immune system even before immunotherapy begins.”

Overacre-Delgoffe’s earlier work had shown that diet and gut microbes can influence cancer patient outcomes and responses to immunotherapy. To investigate their role in treatment side effects, her team fed mice a diet designed to resemble a Western-style human diet, low in fiber and high in fat and processed carbohydrates. The animals began eating it two weeks before checkpoint inhibitor therapy and continued during treatment.

The mice became susceptible to immune-related adverse events and developed immune and microbiome changes resembling many of those seen in affected patients. This gave the researchers a way to test how gut microbes contributed to the inflammation.

Transferring fecal microbes from mice eating the Western-style diet into mice eating a regular, high-fiber diet caused gut inflammation in the recipients. Transfers could also reduce inflammation. Male mice were less susceptible to severe adverse events, and transferring their fecal microbes into female mice reduced the severity of inflammation in the females.

The team also transferred fecal microbes from patients consuming a Western-style diet into germ-free mice, which are raised without microorganisms. Those recipients developed more severe immune-related adverse events. Together, the transfer experiments provided evidence that the microbiome could influence the severity of these reactions in mice.

Within the immune system, the researchers identified a problem involving regulatory T cells. These cells normally suppress excessive immune responses, but stress can make them unstable, a condition called regulatory T cell fragility. Mice eating the Western-style diet showed signs of this fragility during immunotherapy. The researchers found the same instability in regulatory T cells collected from patients with severe immune-related adverse events, but not in cells from patients without the side effect.

Blocking an immune-signaling protein specifically on regulatory T cells restored their stability in mice and reversed inflammation. Switching the animals to a high-fiber diet or giving them supplements containing metabolites, substances produced through metabolism, also stabilized the cells. Restoring stability significantly reduced the severity of adverse events, supporting the interpretation that regulatory T cell fragility is a major underlying cause in this model.

“We were able to generate the first of its kind preclinical mouse model of adverse events that didn’t require full gene knockouts,” said Overacre-Delgoffe. “By combining this novel preclinical model alongside patient data, we were able to identify a very new mechanism of adverse events that hopefully will result in new targeted therapies, allowing more cancer patients to stay on treatment and out of the hospital.”

The model will give researchers a platform to investigate why some patients develop severe reactions and to identify biological markers that might predict susceptibility. Future work will explore drug targets in specific tissues that could limit or eliminate these side effects without disrupting immunotherapy. Metabolite supplementation is another potential approach to reducing susceptibility without interfering with the microbiome, although its promise here comes from experiments in mice.

“We now have some potential targets that we’re going after that seem to limit immune-related adverse events without negatively impacting immunotherapy, which would be the first of its kind and is quite exciting” Overacre-Delgoffe said.

Reference: “Lifestyle-induced regulatory T cell fragility primes adverse events after immune checkpoint blockade” by Dipyaman Patra, Katelyn Wolfgang, Chenxian Ye, Lora Rigatti, Kelsey Ertwine, Kristin M. Morder, Jessica Jana, Ishita Baral, Drew Hurd, Kaitlin Bossong, Steven Mullett, Yingtong Dou, Stacy Gelhaus, Dario A.A. Vignali, Diwakar Davar, Anthony R. Cillo, Greg M. Delgoffe and Abigail E. Overacre-Delgoffe, 22 October 2026, Cell. DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.055

Archaeologists found a small cemetery full of high-status burials, two of which may be the graves of Germanic chieftains.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists excavating in northeastern France have unearthed a small fifth-century cemetery containing the graves of two Germanic chieftains and two warhorses. The burial ground is providing new information about the transitional period after the fall of the Roman Empire.

The burial complex was discovered near the city of Colmar, just a few miles from the Rhine River, which forms the border between France and Germany. This area had a Gallo-Roman village from the first to the third centuries, and archaeologists found several ancient houses, hearths, wells and craft areas, according to a Nov. 6 translated statement from the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research (Inrap).

Archaeologists also uncovered a rare fifth-century cemetery at the site, which was used from about A.D. 450 to 500, a critical time period in Western Europe because of the collapse of the Roman Empire. While scholars have debated for centuries about why the empire fell, one key issue was the repeated occupation of Rome in the fifth century by Germanic tribes known as the Goths and the Vandals.

Several of the burials included gold-and-garnet accessories on weapons and clothing.

Archaeologists discovered 11 adult graves, three graves of children and two horse burials at the site, according to the statement. In two of the female burials, archaeologists found silver bird-shaped brooches, glass bead necklaces and a bone comb, suggesting that these may have been high-status women.

But two of the male burials, in particular, stood out because of their high-quality grave goods, including a sword with a partially preserved wooden scabbard, a shield, a javelin and a scramasax, a type of Germanic short sword, which was decorated with a gold-and-garnet accessory. The weapons are characteristic of the burials of Germanic chieftains or mercenaries, according to the archaeologists, and two horses were buried nearby with their harnesses.

Two horse burials were discovered in the cemetery.

In addition to the weapons and warhorses, archaeologists noticed evidence on the men's bones that hinted that the individuals were likely warriors. Two people suffered stab wounds that showed no signs of healing, which suggests they died quickly and violently, according to the statement. And another man's right knee bones had completely fused together, which would have prevented him from bending it. This condition, called ankylosis, commonly results from an improperly healed injury.

The archaeologists believe the warrior's grave goods weren't just for show, but further study of the skeletons is planned to confirm whether the injuries seen during the excavation could have been sustained in a conflict.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Few Germanic settlements and cemeteries from the fifth century have been found, so the newly excavated site should provide important information about the upheavals linked to the fall of the Western Roman Empire and how that political collapse affected communities on the edge of the empire.

#6415. Vaccinating moms before they give birth saves their babies from dangerous infections

Offspring whose mothers got a Klebsiella vaccine survived a lethal infection, and the antibodies in her milk lasted six weeks.

Newborns arrive with almost no immune defenses of their own. A bacterium called Klebsiella pneumoniae kills thousands of them every year in low- and middle-income countries. It resists a growing list of antibiotics, and no Klebsiella vaccine exists.

So researchers vaccinated the mothers instead, in mice. Pups from unvaccinated mothers almost all died, whereas 80 percent of those from vaccinated mothers survived.

The protection came from antibodies the mothers passed on through the placenta and their milk. It was still working six weeks after birth, by which point the pups’ antibody levels had fallen low. The work is in mice.

David A. Rosen led the study at WashU Medicine, where he is an associate professor of pediatrics and of molecular microbiology.

He worked with Drew Schwartz, whose lab studies the microbiome in newborn sepsis. Paeton Wantuch, a staff scientist in the Rosen lab was the paper’s first author. Rosen said a vaccine for pregnant women is several steps away.

Sepsis is the body’s extreme reaction to an infection that has reached the blood. In low- and middle-income countries, Klebsiella pneumoniae causes more of it in newborns than any other pathogen.

In one survey of seven such countries, 85 percent of the bacteria collected from sick newborns carried genes that disable common antibiotics.

Antibiotics are failing worldwide, and Klebsiella strains that resist a further class of them now infect about three in every 1,000 babies in neonatal intensive care. Up to a quarter of those infants die.

A 2023 modeling study in PLOS Medicine estimated that a maternal Klebsiella vaccine could prevent 80,000 to 400,000 newborn deaths a year.

The vaccine targets the sugar coat that wraps each Klebsiella cell. Two coat types, called K1 and K2, were each linked to a harmless carrier protein, which teaches the immune system to recognize the sugar.

Omniose, a St. Louis startup, built both vaccines, and four of the paper’s authors hold a financial stake in the company.

Female mice received a first dose on the day they were paired with males. Some got one booster two weeks later, and others got boosters at one week and two weeks. A third group received the carrier protein alone.

By day 21, the two-dose and three-dose mothers had made similar amounts of antibody against the sugar coat. That matters for people, the authors wrote, because follow-up visits in pregnancy are hard to guarantee.

Pups born to vaccinated mothers had the antibody against the sugar coat in their blood from birth, and it was still detectable at six weeks of age.

Antibodies reach a baby before birth through the placenta and afterward through milk, so the team collected milk from nursing mothers about eight days after the pups were born.

The team used a human breast pump modified to fit a mouse. The milk held the same antibody the mothers had in their blood, and none of the antibody type that dominates human breast milk.

The authors flagged that difference as one reason mouse results won’t translate directly.

At two weeks old, each pup was injected with enough Klebsiella to kill it. The K1 strain killed every pup whose mother had received the carrier protein alone. More than 80 percent of the pups whose mothers got the K1 vaccine lived, whether she had two doses or three.

Fewer than 35 percent of control pups survived K2, compared with more than 80 percent of pups from K2-vaccinated mothers. The vaccine made the difference, and the number of doses did not. Groups ran from 11 to 30 pups.

Pups from the same mothers were weaned at three weeks and infected at six weeks, alongside female mice that had never been vaccinated. Every pup from a K1-vaccinated mother survived, compared with 40 to 60 percent of the unvaccinated mice.

For K2, pups of three-dose mothers all survived, while the two-dose group’s 70 percent survival was close enough to the unvaccinated mice’s 30 percent that chance can’t be ruled out.

In an interview with Earth.com, Rosen said the last result was the one he hadn’t expected.

“I was somewhat surprised that the vaccines we tested in our model worked even after the pups were six weeks old,” he said.

“The pups had very low detectable antibodies against Klebsiella by this timepoint, but they were still largely immune to Klebsiella infection.”

The authors listed the gaps themselves. Most newborn sepsis strikes in the first week of life, and these pups were infected at two weeks.

The two strains came from human patients but not from newborns, and K1 in particular is rare in newborn sepsis.

The researchers injected bacteria directly into the abdomen. This skipped the gut, the typical starting point for most real infections.

And every pup was born at full term. Many human cases are premature babies, and the authors wrote that a mother’s antibodies may not reach a preterm infant in time.

Rosen told Earth.com the next steps are choosing the best mix of targets, then testing safety in people who are not pregnant, then in pregnant women.

A large final trial would come last, and he said it would need governments across Africa and Asia and funders such as the Gates Foundation.

He added that the risk of any one pregnant woman’s baby getting sick from Klebsiella is still relatively low. “This means that a phase 3 study would require a very large population to determine if a vaccine really works,” he said.

Rosen said Acinetobacter and E. coli also sicken and kill many babies, and vaccines against them could one day be combined into a single shot given during pregnancy.

For now, the team is testing updated vaccines built to cover more of the drug-resistant Klebsiella strains found around the world.

Whether a mother’s antibodies can protect a baby in its first week, when most of these infections happen, is the question the mouse model hasn’t tested yet.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6414. More Than a Billion Years of Earth’s History Is Missing – Scientists May Finally Know Why

Earth’s rocks are missing more than a billion years of history in some places, and the slow rise and fall of continents may explain how those chapters disappeared.

A study led by University of Wollongong (UOW) PhD candidate Santosh Dhungana suggests that the slow rise and fall of continents helped create the Great Unconformity, a vast gap in Earth’s geological record. Published in Nature, the research links this missing history to currents of hot rock in the mantle that moved continents vertically over hundreds of millions of years.

Normally, rock layers preserve a sequence of events, with younger deposits accumulating above older ones. At the Great Unconformity, that sequence jumps: sedimentary rocks from around the beginning of the Cambrian period, roughly 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite more than a billion years old.

“Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth’s story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren’t lost by chance,” Dhungana said.

The Grand Canyon exposes one of the most striking examples of this geological gap. It lies within what was once the ancient continent Laurentia (modern North America). Similar boundaries appear in Europe, Australia, Africa, and Asia, although the missing intervals vary from about 200 million years to well over a billion.

Explaining the Great Unconformity requires accounting for both the removal of rock and the survival of the eroded surface beneath younger deposits. Dhungana said that although scientists had offered several explanations, those ideas had not been thoroughly tested against Earth’s behavior over time.

To investigate, he and his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, modeled mantle convection across hundreds of millions of years. The mantle consists of hot, solid rock that flows very slowly. Its currents can gently lift enormous stretches of land or allow them to sink.

The models indicated that mantle currents raised the ancient continental cores of Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe), and North China during the Neoproterozoic Era, from about one billion to 540 million years ago. This prolonged uplift would have exposed rock to erosion. The era was followed by the Cambrian period, when animal life diversified dramatically.

The next stage helped preserve what erosion had left behind. During the Phanerozoic eon, which spans the past 540 million years, the continental cores gradually sank. Seas spread across their worn surfaces, and accumulating sediment buried the boundary between the ancient rocks and the younger geological record.

The modeled pattern matched the geography of the evidence. North America, northern Europe, and North China, where the Great Unconformity is especially well preserved and documented, all showed the prolonged rise followed by sinking that the researchers proposed.

“Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface,” Associate Professor Flament said.

“Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed, but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.”

Reference: “The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity” by Santosh Dhungana, and Nicolas Flament, 4 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5

This study was funded by the Australian Research Council.

#6413. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

#6411. Three world champion drone-racing pilots lost to an autonomous drone that sees with just one camera

A drone racing AI from Delft beat three world champion drone pilots in Abu Dhabi, with one camera, a tiny neural network and borrowed hardware.

Beating a human champion at drone racing used to take a stereo camera and a lab fitted with motion-tracking equipment. In Abu Dhabi last year, however, a drone with one ordinary camera beat three former world champions in a row.

Its control network was small enough to run on the flight controller, and it flew on hardware and a track its builders didn’t design.

The team at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands calls the system MonoRace. Stavrow Bahnam and Robin Ferede of the University’s MAVLab led the work, with Christophe De Wagter and Guido de Croon.

Their result suggests that fast, reliable control of autonomous robots doesn’t need more sensors and bigger computers, just better use of small ones.

In an interview with Earth.com, de Croon said the team had no idea beforehand whether its drone would even get close.

“Although we knew our drone was going very fast, we were still surprised that it was not only able to compete with a world-champion-level human pilot, but even to win,” he said.

The Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League and the Drone Champions League ran the race in April 2025 with a $1 million prize pool.

Every autonomous team flew the same organizer-built drone, with one rolling-shutter camera and the motion sensors on its flight controller. No GPS, no external tracking and no hardware changes were allowed.

The indoor hall measured 328 feet by 98 feet (100 by 30 meters), and the track ran twice through 11 square gates with openings of about 5 feet (1.5 meters).

One stretch was a split-S, a dive through an upper gate and straight back through a lower one the opposite way.

Human pilots, who fly with video goggles and need lightning-fast reflexes, raced in the same hall on the same dates. The best of them met the best autonomous drones in a knockout of quarterfinal, semifinal and final.

The Delft autonomous drone won all three rounds. Its fastest run took 16.56 seconds, and it reached about 62 miles per hour (100 kilometers per hour).

De Croon told Earth.com that in the first match, the human pilot spotted the Delft drone and reacted to avoid it. The team thinks that cost the pilot a little time.

“At the same time, our AI was oblivious of any other drones, just flying as fast as possible,” he said.

Most drones steer through layers of AI and conventional controllers, each translating a plan into smaller commands. MonoRace skips them.

A neural network of three layers with 64 neurons each takes the drone’s estimated position and motion and sends commands straight to the four motors, 500 times a second. A motor can go from idle to full power in two thousandths of a second.

The network learned to fly in simulation, by trial and error. The simulated drone’s properties were randomized by up to 50 percent so the real one would fall inside what the network had practiced.

On the fastest lap, the measured forces ran at the edge of a 30 percent band around the model and sometimes past it, and the drone kept flying.

More aggressive versions flew faster laps and crashed more. The most reliable one finished 38 of 43 flights.

“Instead of first planning a desired flight path and conventional commands, our neural network learns to directly control the motors,” Ferede said.

At 62 miles per hour, the camera’s images arrive blurred and warped, and a second neural network has to find the gates in them 90 times a second.

A model of how the drone moves fills in between frames. The drone then compares where it expects each gate to appear with where the camera actually finds it.

The comparison also replaced the missing tracking system. The camera’s flexible 3D-printed mount shifted after every crash or repair, so the team flew a lap and then tuned the camera angles until the predicted and observed gates matched.

De Croon said this is how people learn too, predicting what will happen and comparing it with what they see.

The competition hardware caused trouble of its own. Long camera cables flexed under hard acceleration and picked up interference, corrupting between 8 and 75 percent of the images in 10 recorded flights.

The drone still completed the full two-lap track with half its frames corrupted.

One flight, with three-quarters of its images corrupted, flew more than 82 feet (25 meters) blind, cleared one gate and hit the next.

The accelerometer maxed out at 16 times gravity in the sharpest turns, which threw off the position estimate and caused two crashes. The fix was to trust the drone’s own physics model instead of the sensor until the readings came back.

The system still relies on square gates to know where it is, and it can’t see other drones. In a four-drone race it took off first and pulled ahead, then flew into a competitor while lapping it and finished third.

The system also assumes it knows the map of the track in advance.

De Croon said the next step is to replace the hand-built middle of the pipeline, where the drone works out its position, with a neural network as well.

That would let the learning process improve the position estimate itself, and he expects that to make the drone more reliable first and faster later.

He also said that the same, small network could be trained to save energy instead of time. Most machines run on tiny processors with simple controllers that work but are far from optimal, and he thinks energy-optimal control on those chips could save a lot of energy.

The researchers wrote that the approach could carry over to self-driving cars, mobile robots and humanoid systems, though the study tested only the racing drone.

The full study was published in the journal Science Robotics.

#6410. Children are not actually more creative than adults but they are way more confident

Blind judges scored adults as more creative than preschoolers on every task, yet most adults still believe children are more creative.

Most adults, when asked whether preschoolers or grown-ups are more creative, pick the children. When both were put to the test, the adults produced the more creative work on every task.

The children won on something else though: more enjoyment, more self-trust, less worry. That confidence may be what adults mistake for talent.

Janika Saretzki and Mathias Benedek of the Department of Psychology at the University of Graz in Austria ran the comparison. Their co-authors were Ines Fratzl of Graz and Baptiste Barbot of UCLouvain in Belgium and the Yale Child Study Center.

They tested 92 preschoolers, from nine kindergartens, in their last year before school. Most of them were five or six years old.

The 70 adults were mostly in their 20s. Each person was tested alone for about half an hour between August 2021 and April 2022.

Because the two groups were compared once, at one age each, the study can’t say how any one person’s creativity changes as they grow up.

In an interview with Earth.com, Benedek said the ratings ran against his own expectation. “I had assumed children might produce highly unusual ideas that were less appropriate or useful,” he said.

“Instead, adults’ ideas were both more unusual and more effective.”

The first task gave everyone a real tin can to hold and three minutes to name as many creative uses for it as they could, out loud.

The second handed out a sheet of paper and colored pens and asked for a free drawing, framed as play rather than a test, with no time limit mentioned. The third was a test: draw a fantasy animal that doesn’t exist, in up to eight minutes.

After each task, everyone answered five questions on a scale marked with smiley faces. The questions covered how much fun the task was, how much they liked it, and how sure they felt beforehand.

Two more asked how well they thought they had done and how worried they were about doing badly.

Parents reported how often their children did something creative, such as pretend play, in their free time. The adults reported on themselves.

Five experienced raters then scored all 670 tin-can ideas and 324 drawings without knowing whose they were. Each one got a mark for novelty, for effectiveness, and for overall creativity.

On the tin can and the fantasy animal, the adults’ work was rated more novel, more effective and more creative than the children’s.

In the free drawing, the adults still scored higher on effectiveness and creativity. The two groups tied on novelty there, because adults tended to pick the same everyday subjects children did.

The adult lead was widest on effectiveness in the fantasy-animal task, the one that asked outright for something new.

The children also finished faster, spending about two minutes on the three-minute tin-can task against roughly two minutes and 40 seconds for the adults.

On the fantasy animal, the children were done in under three minutes while the adults took six and a half. On the free drawing, with no clock, both groups drew for four to five minutes. Adjusting for the time spent didn’t change the pattern.

Asked by Earth.com what else in the study deserved attention, Benedek pointed to the shape of the tasks. “The adult advantage was clearest in structured tasks with a defined goal,” he said.

Everything the children reported about their own experience ran the other way. They were more motivated on the tin can and the free drawing, more sure of themselves going into both drawing tasks, and less anxious about the tin can.

On all three tasks, they rated their own performance higher than the adults rated theirs, showing a confidence that the adults didn’t match.

The children had more fun on the tin can and the free drawing too. The fantasy animal was the exception: children and adults enjoyed that one about equally.

“Children enjoyed the open-ended tasks more, but in the structured drawing task their enjoyment was no higher than adults’,” Benedek said.

When asked to rate their own creativity, most children picked the top of the scale.

“So children’s creative strength seems to lie in the confidence and motivation they bring to the task, whereas adults feel more comfortable with clear task goals,” said Benedek.

The children also practiced more. Most did something creative nearly every day, by their parents’ account, while the adults most often said about once a week.

Of the 70 adults, 78.6 percent said children are the more creative group. Only 12.9 percent picked adults, and the rest couldn’t choose.

The children themselves were split almost evenly, with 46.7 percent naming children and 43.5 percent naming adults.

The adult belief is not an Austrian quirk. The authors wrote that international surveys find 68 to 77 percent of people agree children are more creative. Among teachers surveyed in the United States and Japan, 63 to 68 percent agree.

Benedek has a reading of why the belief survives. “Most likely because children visibly engage in creative activities, like pretend play, of their own accord in their leisure time,” he said.

“That enthusiasm is easy to see and easy to mistake for greater creative ability,” he added.

The authors put it in one comparison: a “sporty” person, they wrote, is usually someone who plays sports regularly rather than someone who wins competitions.

A caution goes with the children’s answers about fun and confidence.

Young children tend to pick the extreme ends of a rating scale, the authors wrote, and their grasp of a word like “creativity” is still forming. Those self-reports are the softest numbers in the study.

Every participant did the three tasks in the same order, so tiredness could have shaped the later ones. Adults judged all the work, and children might have judged children’s drawings differently.

The raters didn’t know who made each drawing, but a five-year-old’s drawing can look like a five-year-old’s, and the authors wrote that the raters may sometimes have guessed.

Only one narrow age band in one country was tested. The study also didn’t record what the adults did for a living or whether any had trained in an art. How much that training matters is an open question.

In Benedek’s view, the practical lesson runs toward the adults. “Preschoolers enjoy creating without worrying about what others will think of their ideas,” he told Earth.com.

“Adults could often benefit from that kind of playful, judgment-free attitude, at least in the early stages of coming up with ideas.”

Adults in this study rated their own creativity lower than the children rated theirs, and the study can’t say which group had it right.

The next step, the authors wrote, is to find out which it is: a real decline with age, or simply a more accurate view of themselves.

Benedek and his colleagues also want to show these results to adults who picked the children and ask them to explain the choice.

Until then, the authors’ best guess is that children look more creative because they so plainly enjoy creating.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.

#6408. New underwater discoveries in Australia show how First Peoples lived before the ocean swallowed their land

Divers found 21 stone tools on the seabed off Australia, including some made of stone carried 14 miles to a freshwater spring that is now 40 feet under water.

The seabed off a coast looks like the last place an archaeologist would dig. Yet when the last Ice Age ended and the oceans rose, the coast people had lived on for tens of thousands of years went under, stone tools and all.

Off northwestern Australia, divers have now found 21 stone tools on the seafloor. They lie at two spots that were dry land until about 9,000 years ago.

Almost half the tools at one site were made of a rock from an island at the far edge of the archipelago.

That rock outcrops only about 14 miles (23 kilometers) away. Someone carried that stone across a landscape that is now open water. Its destination was a freshwater spring that now lies 40 feet (12 meters) down.

Jonathan Benjamin, a marine archaeologist at Flinders University, led the work, with colleagues at the University of Western Australia, James Cook University and the University of York.

Rangers from the Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation dived alongside them, and two are co-authors on the research paper. The scientists state that they can’t date the tools directly, so 9,000 years is a floor, not an age.

The Ngarda-Ngarli people have cared for Murujuga, also called the Dampier Archipelago, for at least 50,000 years. It was listed as a World Heritage site in 2025. On land it holds more than 4,000 recorded sites, from stone scatters to rock art.

The first underwater finds there came in 2020. The two new sites extend the record offshore and down.

One is a submerged freshwater spring in Flying Foam Passage, about a quarter mile (400 meters) from today’s shoreline. It is a depression 525 feet (160 meters) long, with rock walls up to 8 feet (2.5 meters) high.

The other is a boulder-strewn knoll called the Maitland River Hummock. It is on the bank of a drowned river channel, nearly a mile (1.3 kilometers) from the nearest island.

Both sites were drowned by the same rising sea, roughly a thousand years apart. The knoll would have been a small, rocky island by about 10,000 years ago and was under water soon after.

The spring went under around 9,000 years ago, when rising seas spilled over the sill at the passage’s northern end.

Divers worked the sites on neap tides, when currents in the passages are weakest, for about 40 minutes per dive.

Every rock is coated in marine growth. A diver had to judge shape and angle by eye, lift a candidate stone tool, and send it up.

At the spring, eight dives produced 158 rocks hauled to the surface. After a soak in diluted acid to strip the growth, nine proved to be artifacts: three whole flakes, five broken ones, and a core with at least 12 flake scars.

Most of what a diver lifts turns out to be just a rock.

The knoll was richer. Fourteen dives there produced 12 artifacts, including two cores from which 16 and 19 flakes had been struck.

Murujuga Ranger Malik Churnside, trained as a scientific diver, found one of the knoll’s artifacts himself. Two of the 21 pieces are not pictured in the paper, at the direction of Murujuga Elders.

“The collaboration demonstrates the value of working beside trained Indigenous Rangers who actively contributed to this challenging scientific research,” Benjamin said.

The team read each stone tool’s chemistry with a handheld X-ray fluorescence scanner. Two elements, titanium and zirconium, were plotted against the known rock types of the archipelago. The signal survived thousands of years under the sea.

At the spring, 56 percent of the tools were the local granophyre, a granite-like rock found on both sides of the passage. The other 44 percent were a volcanic sedimentary rock that, today, outcrops only on or near Rosemary Island, about 14 miles (23 kilometers) away.

The knoll told a different story. All 12 of its tools were local rock, probably quarried from the outcrop itself or from an island 2 miles (3.5 kilometers) north.

So the spring looks like a gathering place, where people arrived carrying tools made elsewhere. The knoll looks like a quarry beside a river.

On land, nearby sites that became islands when the sea rose show mostly local stone, which fits a world where the long walks had ended.

The artifacts lie loose on the seafloor, with no buried layers or charcoal to date. Their true age could be anywhere from 9,000 years back to the 50,000-year record of the wider region.

Their edges are slightly rounded by sand, but current meters show the tides move sand, not rocks this size.

The samples are small, 12 tools at the knoll and 17 at the two spring sites. An unmapped outcrop of the island rock could also sit closer on the seabed than the geology on land suggests, though the team considers the known map reliable.

Vincent Adams, director of the Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation, said the finds change the map of what needs protecting.

“What this research shows is that our cultural landscape extends far beyond the shoreline and into Sea Country, where important parts of our story remain preserved beneath the sea,” he said.

Everything found so far lies inside the 100-foot (30-meter) depth contour. The drowned coast runs out to about 425 feet (130 meters), where the oldest material should be.

Reaching it will take bigger boats and faster ways to tell a tool from a rock. The team wrote that both are on the agenda.

The full study was published in the journal Quaternary Science Reviews.
