#6407. People lost the same amount of weight drinking water or diet beverages in a two year study

A two-year study of 493 adults showed that people lose about the same amount of weight whether they drink water or diet beverages.

If you are trying to lose weight, choosing diet drinks over water will not make a huge difference. In a two-year study of 493 adults, participants who drank diet beverages and people who drank water showed very similar weight loss results.

All participants followed a weight-management program and drank at least two 11-fluid-ounce (330-milliliter) servings a day of their assigned drink.

Those still enrolled at two years had lost 10.6 pounds (4.8 kilograms) with diet drinks and 8.2 pounds (3.7 kilograms) with water.

The difference between the groups was not statistically significant. Only 220 of the 493 participants completed the trial.

The SWITCH trial was run at the University of Liverpool in England. Participants lived within 50 miles (80 kilometers) of Merseyside and began their trial drinks between July 2016 and December 2021.

The trial enrolled adults aged 18 to 65 with a body mass index of 27 to 35. They were randomly assigned to water (246 people) or diet drinks (247 people).

Their average age was about 45, and roughly seven in ten were women. The investigators supplied the drinks, which the sponsor paid for.

The diet group chose from 20 branded beverages containing the artificial sweeteners aspartame, acesulfame potassium or sucralose. The water group drank bottled spring or mineral water and was asked to avoid diet drinks.

For 12 weeks, participants attended weekly group sessions led by nutritionists. Monthly sessions followed for 40 weeks, and the final 52 weeks were unassisted.

Advice covered healthy eating and cutting sugar. During the first year, participants were also asked to add ten minutes of daily walking until they reached 60 minutes on six days a week.

The main analysis covered the 220 people with weight data at both the start and week 104. Of those, 117 drank water and 103 drank diet beverages.

Two other analyses that accounted for dropouts also found no significant difference. One used multiple imputation, and the other carried forward each person’s last recorded weight.

After the first 12 weeks, weight loss was equivalent with either drink. Water drinkers had lost 12.3 pounds (5.6 kilograms) and diet-drink users 12.8 pounds (5.8 kilograms), a 2023 report on the trial found.

At one year, diet-drink users had lost significantly more weight in the main analysis, though the gap was not clinically meaningful. By two years, the gap was no longer significant.

Professor Jo Harrold, dean of psychology at the University of Liverpool, led the trial.

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial,” Harrold explained.

Waist and hip measurements fell in both groups, with no difference between them.

Total cholesterol rose more with diet drinks. Blood sugar, measured as HbA1c, and diastolic blood pressure fell more with water, but none of these differences was judged clinically meaningful.

Hunger rose slightly over two years, whichever drink people had. The increase was significant only in the diet-drink group, and the difference between groups was not significant.

Sugar intake fell with either drink, slightly more with diet beverages. Total sweetener intake fell significantly only among water drinkers.

Professor Jason Halford, a co-author at the University of Leeds and the University of Liverpool, pointed to the length of the trial.

“This study provides the long-term clinical evidence that has been missing from international discussions,” Halford said.

In 2023, the World Health Organization advised against using non-sugar sweeteners (NSS) to control body weight. The recommendation was conditional and does not apply to people who already have diabetes.

The guideline covers sweeteners such as aspartame, sucralose, saccharin, stevia and acesulfame potassium.

It drew on a systematic review that found no long-term benefit for reducing body fat. Possible long-term harms in adults included higher risks of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and death.

“Replacing free sugars with NSS does not help with weight control in the long term,” said Francesco Branca, WHO’s director for nutrition and food safety.

The SWITCH authors argue that the guidance rests mainly on uncertain findings from cohort studies rather than randomized trials.

“We hope this evidence informs future WHO guidance and public health policy,” Harrold noted.

The authors partly blame the low completion rate, about 45 percent, on the COVID-19 pandemic, the two-year length and the voluntary final year. That final year was added by amendment after recruitment fell short.

The trial took place at a single site in England, and data on race and ethnicity were not collected.

About 76 percent of participants already drank diet beverages regularly before joining. The trial compared diet drinks with water, not with sugary drinks.

The American Beverage Association funded the research. The team states that it was independent of the funder and fully controlled the analysis and reporting.

The funder could review the manuscript, though final decisions on content rested with the authors. Several authors also report funding from or ties to beverage or food industry organizations.

The study was published in the journal British Journal of Nutrition.

#6406. Many physicists now believe that gravity and the fabric of the universe are just a giant web of connected quantum information

Two physicists derived Einstein's equations of gravity from a measure of quantum information, a new clue in the search for quantum gravity.

If you open any physics textbook, it will tell you that gravity is one of the four fundamental forces of nature. However, two scientists have just shown that Einstein’s math for gravity can actually be explained by something that isn’t a force in the first place.

They start with a measure of how easily they can tell apart a patch of space holding matter and a patch of empty space.

If the argument holds, the curving of space and time isn’t a starting point. It is a consequence of how quantum information is arranged.

Philipp Dorau and Albert Much of Leipzig University in Germany published the work in March. It is a mathematical argument, not an experiment, and it rests on simplifying assumptions the authors spell out.

“It is a little like plucking a guitar string: matter is the pluck, spacetime is the string, and the note it produces is Einstein’s equations,” said Much, an assistant professor of quantum field theory and general relativity and a co-author of the study.

In 1995, the physicist Ted Jacobson showed that Einstein’s equations could be derived from the physics of heat and entropy.

The laws describing a gas emerge from the motion of its molecules. Gravity, he suggested, might emerge from something deeper in the same way.

Jacobson’s version used classical thermodynamics, the science of heat flowing between warm and cold things. Dorau and Much wanted the same result using only quantum field theory, the mathematics that describes matter at the smallest scales.

For that they needed a different kind of entropy. The usual quantum measure of disorder gives infinite answers for a sharply defined region of space, because entanglement between neighboring points never stops at small scales.

The quantity they used instead is called relative entropy. It measures how well two quantum states can be distinguished from each other, and it stays finite.

Here is one way to picture it. Imagine the surface of the sea, which is never perfectly still. Its constant rippling is like the quantum vacuum, the state physicists call empty space.

Now imagine a wave passing across that surface. Relative entropy tells you how well you can distinguish the wave from the rippling background.

The two physicists worked out this quantity at a horizon. Any small patch of curved space contains one, in the form seen by an observer who keeps accelerating.

“We show that this quantity, evaluated at a horizon – a boundary in spacetime beyond which no information can be received – equals the energy flowing across that horizon,” Much said.

The last step borrows a rule from black holes. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking argued that the entropy of a black hole grows with the area of its horizon rather than its volume.

Dorau and Much assume that same entropy-area rule holds for their local horizons. Relative entropy equals the energy crossing the horizon, that energy sets how much the horizon’s area changes, and Einstein’s equations follow with no extra ingredients.

With the black hole value for that rule, the usual constant in front of the equations comes out right. Furthermore, second free constant appears, which the authors identify with the cosmological constant.

However, the authors are careful about what they have shown. “Most of the ingredients for our work have been known for decades,” said Dorau, a theoretical physicist at Leipzig’s Institute for Theoretical Physics.

“It was recent progress in understanding relative entropy that gave us the missing link between quantum information, thermodynamics, and gravity.”

The derivation treats matter in its simplest form, as the smallest possible disturbance of empty space. It works only to a first approximation.

The paper says a fully rigorous treatment would have to track smaller corrections, which the authors expect to be technically demanding.

It also leans on the equivalence principle, Einstein’s rule that any small enough region of curved space behaves like flat space. And the entropy-area relation at the heart of the final step is assumed, not derived.

What comes out at the end is the semiclassical form of Einstein’s equations, in which spacetime stays classical while matter is quantum.

That isn’t yet a theory of quantum gravity, the long-sought merger of Einstein’s gravity with quantum theory. Furthermore, whether the same reasoning survives when matter takes more complicated forms is still an open question.

The two physicists plan to try. They want to extend the argument to other kinds of quantum matter, to more general quantum states, and to light-like surfaces, which are central to black hole physics.

“We are currently trying to generalize this to full quantum gravity, and it seems to me that this connection that we have identified will serve as a testbed for the various theories of quantum gravity,” Much said.

The full study was published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

#6404. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

W. Xin et al. Overcoming environmental constraints: octopus uses 3-step or 4-step strategies to squeeze through small holes. Journal of Experimental Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1242/jeb.252825

#6403. Fake rocks are helping rare Australian snakes survive in the wild after builders took their natural homes

At least four out of six broad-headed snakes, raised in captivity then released under artificial rocks, survived their first months.

For years, people have taken natural sandstone from the Australian bush for landscaping. This practice leaves broad-headed snakes without homes.

To address the problem, scientists released six captive-bred snakes back into the wild in May 2026, giving them human-made rocks to live under.

According to the University of Technology Sydney (UTS), this world-first release is working, with at least four of the snakes surviving their first few months.

Six animals is a tiny sample, the count is preliminary, and neither official announcement cites a published or peer-reviewed paper. Yet the scientists behind the study are encouraged.

UTS wildlife ecologist Jonathan Webb leads the program with Aussie Ark and the Traditional Owners of the Shoalhaven. His own field site is a population in Morton National Park, south of Sydney, and he has been counting snakes there for 34 years.

Webb started on the snake during his PhD at the University of Sydney. The species had once been common around Sydney. By the 1990s it was rare, while other snakes were doing fine.

He kept monitoring after the PhD and joined UTS in 2012. “It turned into a long-term study purely by accident,” he said of the 34 years. Internship students still go out with him on the surveys each year.

The snake has a flattened head and a black body with yellow bands, and it grows to about 35 inches (90 centimeters). It lives only on the rocky escarpment of the Sydney sandstone basin and the ranges around it.

Its life runs slowly. A broad-headed snake can take five years to reach adulthood. Females reproduce only every two or three years, and wild adults can reach 23.

Young snakes depend on rock outcrops for shelter and for food, because they eat only small rock-dwelling lizards such as geckos and skinks. Webb said that removing the rocks takes away both.

The state of New South Wales listed bushrock removal as a key threatening process in a final determination dated November 5, 1999. The document names Hoplocephalus bungaroides, the broad-headed snake, among the threatened animals affected.

Webb said the rules need enforcing. He wants a permit system that makes sellers prove their rocks did not come from areas with threatened species.

Landscape suppliers still sell boulders taken from the bush, he said, and a feature boulder can fetch 450 Australian dollars. He called that “really frustrating.”

Weather and fire added to the damage. His monitoring recorded a decline during the 2017-19 drought. Little breeding followed for three years after the 2020 bushfires. By 2023 the population had dropped by around 64 percent.

Aussie Ark secured 17 wild adult snakes in October 2024 to start the captive side of the program. That group later grew to 20 and lives in terrariums at Conservation Ark in Somersby, New South Wales.

Earlier in 2026 the program recorded the first captive birth of the species, Aussie Ark said. A few weeks later, remote-sensor cameras filmed a live birth, which the group described as never documented before.

Eight juveniles have been bred so far. Two stayed in the captive group because of their genetics, and six went to the release sites. Aussie Ark project lead Dylan Wallis and Chief Conservation Officer Hayley Shute let one of them go together.

Each snake carries a unique marking on its head, so staff can identify individual animals during later checks. Captive programs are helping other Australian species too. The University of Newcastle reported a first captive breeding of Littlejohn’s tree frog.

Dr. Benjamin Croak, who completed his PhD at UTS under Webb, developed the artificial rocks. UTS says they have the right crevice size and mimic the thermal properties of natural stone.

The snakes hunt at night and spend the day under rock, which gives them warmth and cover and also draws the lizards they eat, Webb said. He described the artificial versions as “critical to the survival of the juvenile snakes.”

Croak had worked on the species’ shelter needs years earlier. In a 2013 paper in PLOS ONE with Webb and Richard Shine, he reported radio-tracking nine adults in Wollemi and Yengo national parks.

The snakes spent most of winter beneath sun-warmed rocks. The authors recommended that managers keep existing surface rock in place.

The program also trains and supports Indigenous rangers to monitor the snakes on Country. Traditional Owner Frank Connolly Jr. said the snake is “important to our culture” and that young people are learning the work for the next generation.

UTS, in its note of November 6, says at least four of the six survived the first few months. That is the only survival figure in the official announcements. Aussie Ark’s release note says the six went out under artificial rocks but gives no survival count.

The figure is a minimum from a very small group, a few months after release. UTS says Webb’s team has run fortnightly surveys. Neither note gives the survey results or the date each snake was last seen.

The announcements also describe no comparison group of snakes released without artificial rocks. Webb’s view that the rocks made the difference therefore remains an expert judgment, and UTS still calls the release a pilot study.

Predators are an early risk. Webb named kookaburras and brown snakes among native hunters, along with invasive cats and foxes. In South Australia, researchers confirmed that feral cats killed 74 of 389 reintroduced animals at two sites.

Breeding in the wild is further off. Adulthood can take five years, so the released juveniles have a long wait before they can add to any population. Pressures on snakes worldwide, such as habitat loss, continue in the meantime.

Webb said the focus for the next few years will be restoring habitat and releasing more captive-bred snakes at selected sites. Aussie Ark founder Tim Faulkner said the group had spent years “navigating so much red tape” to reach the first release.

One of Webb’s first memories is sitting on his dad’s shoulder while the kid next door let him touch a green tree snake. Going out to check the young broad-headed snakes under their artificial rocks, he said, “I feel like a kid again.”

The information was obtained from the University of Technology Sydney.

Neuroscientists say people can be "trained" to recognize when they're dreaming — in other words, lucid dreaming may be an acquirable skill.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During dreams, bizarre scenes you encounter can seem as tangible as reality; you feel as though you're really flying through the sky or being chased through a jungle of bright-purple trees. But in special cases, people realize they're in the midst of a dream as it's unfolding.

Called lucid dreaming, this phenomenon occurs when we suddenly regain our capacity for metacognition, or thinking about our own thoughts, in the middle of a dream. Lucid dreamers can sometimes even control the content or trajectory of their dreams. Now, researchers claim that they've found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they're awake.

In a study involving a few dozen participants, the scientists found that repeating this training twice a week for a month significantly increased how often participants experienced lucid dreaming. They say the approach could have practical applications as an intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety or post-traumatic stress disorder — but those applications are theoretical, for now.

#6401. A tiny ocean animal called the leaf sheep figured out how to make its own food from sunlight

The leaf sheep is a sea slug that looks like a cartoon lamb standing in its own pasture. Oddly enough, the pasture is the strange part. The leaf-shaped…

The leaf sheep is a sea slug that looks like a cartoon lamb standing in its own pasture. Oddly enough, the pasture is the strange part.

The leaf-shaped growths on its back are green because the slug keeps chloroplasts, which are the sunlight-capturing parts of the algae it eats. Those chloroplasts go on working inside the leaf sheep for days or longer.

Animals eat food for energy, and plants make their own food from sunlight. A few sea slugs do both, and the best-studied one is a bigger cousin of the leaf sheep, Elysia chlorotica, an emerald green slug from the Massachusetts coast.

In 2008, researchers found one clue to how it manages that, in its own DNA: a working copy of a gene taken from the algae it eats.

The leaf sheep’s scientific name is Costasiella kuroshimae. It is about the size of a grain of rice, according to the World Wildlife Fund, and lives in shallow tropical water around Japan, Indonesia, and the Philippines.

Two ear-shaped feelers above its eyes sense chemicals in the water, and it grazes on an alga called Avrainvillea on shallow reefs and in seagrass beds. The species was first described in 1993.

Mary Rumpho at the University of Maine led the work on the cousin with James Manhart of Texas A&M University. Their team went looking in the slug’s genes.

A chloroplast carries only a small part of its own instructions. Of the 1,000 to 5,000 proteins a chloroplast needs, its own DNA codes for fewer than 10%. The rest come from genes in the algal cell’s nucleus.

So a slug that keeps the chloroplast and loses the rest of the algal cell should end up with chloroplasts that can’t maintain themselves.

E. chlorotica keeps them anyway. A gene passing between an alga and an animal is extremely rare, or at least not well documented, and Rumpho’s team set out to find one.

The slug hatches from eggs that carry no chloroplasts, and its larvae swim free. They won’t change into juveniles without one alga, Vaucheria litorea, which grows in long threads, and the juveniles must feed on it to keep developing.

Young slugs are grayish brown. As they feed, they keep chloroplasts only in the cells lining their branched gut, and as that gut spreads, the whole animal turns green.

The chloroplasts never divide inside the slug, which lives about 10 months. In earlier work, Rumpho’s group had measured oxygen coming off slugs kept from algae for at least five months. The chloroplasts were still photosynthesizing.

The team started with the alga. They read the complete DNA of its chloroplast and found that one gene was missing. It was a gene called psbO.

That gene makes a protein that the photosynthesis process requires in order to split water and release oxygen. Sunlight wears that protein out, so a chloroplast has to keep making more of it.

The algae plant keeps this gene in its main control center, not in the chloroplast. Until now, scientists had never seen an animal naturally possess this gene.

So if the slug’s chloroplasts were still releasing oxygen five months after their last meal of algae, the protein had to be coming from somewhere. The team looked in the slug.

They found the gene there, matching the algal version exactly, and it was switched on.

A leftover bit of algae in the slug’s gut could explain that. So the team checked slug eggs, which carry no chloroplasts and no algae. The eggs had the gene too.

That was the team’s evidence that the gene belongs to the slug itself and gets passed on to its young.

Rumpho’s team also sequenced the slug’s mitochondrial DNA, the small, separate genome that animals carry in their cells. The gene wasn’t there, which left the slug’s nuclear DNA as the likely location.

How did the gene get there? The authors suggested a route. When the slug feeds, algal nuclei come into direct contact with the cells lining its gut.

If a nucleus breaks open there, pieces of algal DNA could be taken up by the slug, or carried across by a virus.

Other algal genes have turned up in the slug too. A year earlier, another group had reported three algal genes in E. chlorotica that code for proteins that help collect light, matching the alga’s almost exactly.

The authors also wrote that the slug adds weight to an idea from biologist Lynn Margulis. New kinds of life, she proposed, can arise when one organism takes in parts and genes from another. They called slugs like this “green animals.”

The team did not find where in the slug’s chromosomes the gene is, what DNA surrounds it, or what switched it on once it arrived. They also did not learn how the protein gets from the slug’s cell into the chloroplast.

The authors wrote that many more algal genes have very likely been transferred to the slug. Reading its whole genome is what it will take to settle where they are.

The study did not ask any of this about the leaf sheep. The next question is whether Costasiella carries an algal gene of its own, and its genome is the place scientists should look next.

The full study was published in the journal PNAS.

#6399. An ancient Roman settlement missing from all history books was found in a Welsh village right before new houses were built

A survey taken before the planned construction of 300 homes at Mancot in Wales led archaeologists to a 2,000-year-old Roman settlement.

In December 2025, archaeologists from Heneb were working on a housing site beside Gladstone Way in Mancot, a village in Flintshire, northeast Wales. Castle Green Homes planned to build 300 houses on the land.

The ground on that plot held a Roman settlement that was completely unknown, never mentioned in historical records.

The site is about 2,000 years old and produced an unusually large collection of Roman metalwork. Heneb published photographs captioned as a Roman brooch casting mold from the dig, and the finds are still being analyzed.

The development is called Gladstone Grange, and Flintshire Council had allocated the land for housing. The developer assessed the site for archaeological value before the project began and hired Heneb, the Trust for Welsh Archaeology, as part of that process.

A geophysical survey, which maps buried features without digging, picked up structures and signs of historic activity under the ground. Heneb then monitored the site before and during the early stages of the work.

The trust says it completed a full investigation of the remains before the site was developed. It announced the find on November 9, 2026, and said the fieldwork has ended.

Excavators uncovered a Romano-British industrial settlement, the term archaeologists use for communities in Britain under Roman rule. It sat inside a network of plot boundaries and drainage systems.

A site plan released by Heneb marks groups of buildings lettered A to H. A large drainage ditch formed the eastern boundary for most of them.

The settlement grew in phases. Timber houses came first, and Heneb says some of them may date to the end of the Iron Age.

By the third century AD, elongated, semi-rectangular buildings had replaced those houses. One photograph from the dig shows the outline of a third-century building in the cleared soil.

Heneb thinks the remains continue west under the part of the village now called Big Mancot. The announcement does not say how far they run.

Heneb lists a wide variety of brooches from Mancot. People in Roman Britain pinned their clothes with them and also wore them as decoration.

The trust published photographs of the objects. One shows a disc brooch set with enamel. Heneb says the decoration appeared only after extensive laboratory conservation.

Another photograph shows an enamelled brooch of the Wirral type. A third shows a large brooch of a kind often found on Anglesey, the Welsh island where detectorists recovered fifteen Iron Age gold coins.

The dig also produced a lead spindle whorl, a weight for spinning thread. A denarius of the emperor Commodus turned up too, and Heneb’s caption dates it to AD 192.

Three more photographs carry the caption “Casting mould of a Roman Brooch.” Heneb does not say whether they show one mold or several.

Heneb says “substantial evidence” suggests the inhabitants made these brooches themselves. The trust thinks they probably worked within “a wider industrial supply network” that served local people and Chester.

Mancot overlooks Chester, site of the Roman legionary fortress of Deva Victrix. Romans built it in the AD 70s and occupied it for more than 300 years. The Twentieth Legion was based there for most of that time, according to Cheshire West and Chester Council.

Very little Roman activity had been recorded in this part of Flintshire. Heneb says the land around Chester has often been described as a “largely undeveloped hinterland,” which is why the trust considers Mancot significant.

Other industrial sites had already turned up elsewhere in north Wales. At Pentre Ffwrndan, near Flint, Roman workers smelted lead ore from Halkyn Mountain from about the mid-60s AD. The former Clwyd-Powys Archaeological Trust, now part of Heneb, says it is likely the lead was shipped to Chester.

Volunteers and archaeologists working there in 2017 and 2018 excavated a Roman road aligned toward a probable quayside on the estuary.

At Prestatyn, bronze smiths, iron smiths and enamellers worked in adjacent timber workshops from about AD 90 or 100 until about AD 160, the national record of Welsh monuments says. A trust leaflet adds that excavators there found slag, bronze scrap and parts of casting molds.

Near Wrexham, a detectorist’s lead ingot led researchers to the first confirmed Roman villa in North Wales. Another detectorist in the region found up to 15,000 Roman coins.

Heneb places Mancot within this emerging pattern and argues that Roman Wales was “far more complex and interconnected than previously understood.”

Heneb’s announcement gives no total for the brooches, the coins or the buildings. It also does not mention furnaces, hearths or metal waste at Mancot, the kinds of remains reported at Prestatyn.

The link to Chester remains an inference, and Heneb words it as a probability. The trust has named no buyer, and the announcement cites no chemical test that ties the metal to the fortress.

The objects are undergoing analysis and conservation. They will then go to Flintshire Museum Services, which plans a public display, though Heneb has given no date.

Heneb has finished digging at Gladstone Grange, where 300 homes are being built. The brooches, the casting finds and the Commodus coin stay with conservators for now.

The information was obtained from Heneb: The Trust for Welsh Archaeology.

#6398. A last minute skeleton discovery finally proved that a Norse church once stood right near Erik the Red’s Greenland settlement

A skeleton found at Qinngua confirms the first Norse church found in Greenland in over 60 years.

In August 2026, archaeologists at Qinngua, near Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland, reached the second-to-last day of their planned excavation timeline.

The National Museum of Denmark first dug at this particular ruin in the 2000s, and none of the work since then had turned up a burial site. Until that fateful day.

Their skeleton discovery confirms that the stone ruin was a Norse church, the first found in Greenland in more than 60 years. Its date is still provisional, and researchers are analyzing samples from the site.

Qinngua lies close to Brattahlíð, the main settlement of Erik the Red. Researchers from Copenhagen’s National Museum worked there with Bergen’s University Museum, Greenland’s National Museum and Archive and UNESCO Kujataa.

Michael Nielsen of the Greenland museum photographed the dig, and Kujataa site manager Aqqaluaq Frederiksen shot the ruin from above.

The ruin consists of a rectangular stone wall with a stone building in the middle. Researchers had suspected a church there for some time because of that layout, which the University of Bergen calls a typical mark of a medieval church.

According to the National Museum’s history pages, Greenland’s oldest churches were small, stood close to farmhouses and had circular churchyard walls. Farmers built them and owned them.

Proof needed a cemetery with graves. Museum teams dug at Qinngua in the 2000s and found none.

This summer the team located a skeleton placed with its head toward the east, which the museum describes as customary for Christian burials. The grave confirmed a cemetery, and the cemetery confirmed the church.

Christian Edelfelt Koch Madsen coordinates research on the project for the National Museum. He called the grave “the smoking gun.” He said, “Now there is no doubt that this is a church.”

Inuit were buried in stone-covered chambers and Norse people in cemeteries, Madsen said, and the written sources point the same way.

Konrad Smiarowski of the University Museum of Bergen co-leads the project. He said in Bergen’s statement that the Norse dead lay in consecrated ground beside churches.

The end of the dig drew many curious locals from the village of Qassiarsuk, according to a caption in the museum’s press pack.

Medieval texts name several Norse churches and say roughly where they stood. Smiarowski said researchers have placed most of them using those texts, especially Flateyjarbók and Ívar Bárðarson’s description of Greenland, along with landscape analysis and known Norse settlements.

One account mentions Kirkja undir Sólarfjöllum, the Church under the Sunny Mountains. The National Museum said this description fits Qinngua rather well.

The mountains behind the site stand right by the ice cap, under a local high-pressure system that often brings sunny weather. The site is in the part of Tunulliarfik Fjord that the Norse knew as Eiriksfjord.

Madsen expects the match to guide future fieldwork. Because this location agrees with the sources, he said, “it would make sense to try to locate other churches also mentioned in writing.”

Researchers have found six churches in the relatively small area around Brattahlíð, and only three remained in use into the Middle Ages. The ruins of two or three farms stand near the new church, which may suggest the beginnings of a village.

The National Museum’s research page on the Norse says farms with a church were central places in a hierarchic society. Other farmers were probably tied to church owners through kinship, religion or tenancy.

Madsen said the cluster near Erik the Red’s seat looks like “a veritable race to build churches and thus demonstrate power and position.” Some builders may have lost that race and given up on their churches, he said, and Qinngua could be one of them.

Smiarowski described churches as centers of power as well as places of worship. Studying them, he said, can show how Norse society handled climatic and social pressures.

Churchyards have been informative in Denmark too, where 77 Viking graves clustered around the lost St. Oluf’s Church in Aarhus.

The Norse held on in Greenland from about 980 until the 1400s. Written sources say Icelanders led by Erik the Red settled the southwest around 985, and that the Western Settlement emptied in the middle of the 14th century.

The last written evidence of life in the Eastern Settlement dates to 1408. Archaeological finds and radiocarbon dates suggest people stayed there until at least the middle of the 15th century.

A Norwegian king appointed a bishop for Greenland in the early 1100s, the National Museum says, but bishops probably did not reach their post at Gardar until the early 1200s. None lived there after Bishop Alf died in 1378.

The churches found 60 years ago dated to the Viking Age and were soon given up. The Qinngua church is bigger and was likely used through the Middle Ages, a period when knowledge is “still full of holes,” the National Museum said.

Lake sediment work has tied the arrival and departure of the Greenland Norse to shifting temperatures. Hemlock and jack pine from five Norse sites in Greenland also point to timber trips to North America.

The institutions have not published a laboratory date. The range of 1100 to 1300 comes from the church’s large size and its many hewn stones, and the arms laid along the sides suggest the early Middle Ages.

The statements describe one skeleton and give no age or sex. They also give no measurements for the building. The announcement came as a press release, without a peer-reviewed paper.

Neither statement reports an inscription or object that names the church, so the link to Kirkja undir Sólarfjöllum rests on the landscape.

The two possible histories of the building also remain open, since the museum describes likely use through the Middle Ages while Madsen suggests its owners may have abandoned it. “More research will show,” he said.

The grave confirmed on that second-to-last day is the the first burial reported at Qinngua at Qinngua. Samples from the find are still being analyzed.

The information was obtained from the National Museum of Denmark.

#6397. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

This tiny inkwell contains an alphabetic inscription in ancient Etruscan, a language that has never been fully decoded.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The chicken-shaped, black-glazed vase has an abecedarium ‪—‬ an inscription with the 26 letters of the Etruscan alphabet in order.

What it is: A bird-shaped ceramic inkwell

This small terra-cotta vase, which is shaped like a cockerel or young male chicken with human feet, was discovered in central Italy and was made by the ancient Etruscans. The potter inscribed the Etruscan alphabet on the body of the chicken, giving modern researchers clues to a language that has never been fully deciphered.

The vase stands just over 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. The dark-black ceramic, known as bucchero, was made through a unique firing method that prevented the kiln from getting enough oxygen, which caused the clay to absorb carbon. Bucchero is considered the trademark Etruscan ceramic, and it was produced from the seventh to the fourth centuries B.C. by this pre-Roman society. It is unclear where the cockerel vase was originally found, but it may have been discovered in a grave in one of the many cemeteries that surround Viterbo, which was originally an Etruscan town about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northwest of modern-day Rome.

According to The Met, the vase may have been a portable inkwell used by an ancient Etruscan who was learning how to write. The cockerel's head was the stopper, and it was loosely attached to the body by a cord through a set of loops. The inscription on the body of the vase is known as an abecedarium ‪—‬ the sequential list of letters in an alphabet.

The Etruscan alphabet is well known, since it was adopted from a regional version of the Greek alphabet in the early eighth century B.C. There were 26 letters in the Etruscan alphabet, but one of them in this abecedarium is incorrect. A close look at the end of the alphabet shows that someone inscribed an S twice; the second one should look more like an X, according to The Met.

The terracotta cockerel vase was one of several ancient Etruscan artifacts that helped experts partially decode the mysterious ancient language, as it preserved the order of the letters in the early alphabet, archaeologist Gisela Richter wrote in a 1930 catalog of The Met's classical artifacts.

Thanks to the adoption of the Greek alphabet, it's possible to fully sound out the Etruscan language. But although more than 10,000 Etruscan inscriptions have been found, the language is still only partially understood because those inscriptions are short and any lengthy Etruscan literature that once existed has been lost.

#6394. New laser mapping tool helps scientists track baby trees and monitor forest regrowth on a massive scale

Culling deer let 2.65 million young trees spread across the Cairngorms, and a laser scan from a plane mapped Scotland's forest recovery.

The Cairngorms, in Scotland’s Highlands, are famous for bare, heather-covered hills. Those hills used to be forest. Woodland once covered half to four-fifths of the country, but only about 4 percent of the native forest is left.

Across one stretch of the Cairngorms, though, the forests are coming back on their own, and a plane carrying a laser scanner has now counted them.

The scan found 2.65 million young trees under 16 feet (5 meters) tall across 220 square miles (569 square kilometers).

About 13,000 acres (5,325 hectares) of open ground now carries enough saplings to count as young woodland. Very little of it was planted. The land managers shot deer instead.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge led the mapping, with partners at RSPB Scotland and Cairngorms Connect, the partnership that manages the land. Sudina Thapa and Aland Chan were the first authors.

The scan is a single snapshot of trees, commissioned in July 2023, and the smallest seedlings, the ones still hidden in the heather, are not in the count.

In an interview with Earth.com, Chan said the scale was what surprised him. “You notice regenerating trees on the ground, but that feels very different from seeing millions of trees plotted on the map,” he said.

Four land managers formed Cairngorms Connect a decade ago, with a 200-year plan to let native forest climb back up to its natural tree line inside the Cairngorms National Park.

Their main tool is culling deer, which eat seedlings before the seedlings can get established. Ecologists have estimated that deer numbers have to fall to roughly 3 to 5 per square kilometer, about 8 to 13 per square mile, before young trees can regenerate.

Across the partnership, densities now average below 4 per square kilometer. That is the threshold the whole plan rests on, and the hills have crossed it.

Young woodland here means more than 100 trees per hectare, about 40 per acre. Of the 6.17 million trees the scan picked out, 43 percent were under 16 feet tall.

The authors wrote that this colonization was largely natural, with small areas of planting where no seed trees were nearby.

Mapping trees from the air with laser scanning is not new. The LiDAR scanner fires pulses at the ground, times the return of each one, and builds a three-dimensional picture of everything below.

This flight, about 2,000 feet (600 meters) up, recorded 22 pulses for every square meter of ground.

The hard part was the small trees. Heather in these hills grows to about 3.6 feet (1.1 meters), and bracken grows taller, so a young pine can be shorter than the shrubs around it.

“We’re not the first study to use LiDAR to map trees, but it’s the first time we’ve used it to map these small, regenerating trees at this scale,” Chan told Earth.com.

The team’s method found trees once they outgrew the heather. Checked against Cairngorms saplings measured on the ground, it caught 83 percent of tree clusters between 4.6 and 5.2 feet (1.4 to 1.6 meters) tall. Above 6 feet (1.8 meters) it caught more than 95 percent.

Trees still under about 3.3 feet (1 meter) were almost all missed.

With every young tree on a map, the team could ask where the forest is spreading and where it isn’t. Distance from existing forest mattered most. The farther a patch of ground was from a seed source, the fewer saplings it held.

Bogs consistently held fewer young trees than dry heathland. Elevation made little difference low down but was more important above about 1,300 feet (400 meters), where the ground approaches the natural tree line.

Where deer had hit hardest in the past, fewer saplings stood now. Parcels rated low or medium for browsing damage in surveys run between 2006 and 2013 carried more young trees than parcels rated high.

One oddity stood out. The parcels rated very high carried more saplings than those rated high. The authors suggested heavy browsing may have opened up the vegetation and exposed bare ground for seeds.

Chan said ecologists have long known that trees regenerate less readily far from seed sources or on boggy ground. Putting a number on how much less, he said, is what makes it possible to model what happens next.

Asked by Earth.com what walkers in the Cairngorms should notice, Chan said Scots pine tends to come back first, with birch and rowan following. A self-seeded forest grows differently from a plantation.

“Instead of dense rows of trees of roughly the same size shading out the entire understory, visitors will see trees of different shapes and sizes scattered across the landscape,” he said.

That mix of shapes and sizes creates more kinds of small habitat for animals, he added.

Capercaillie, a large grouse, and red squirrels are among the species now confined to the remaining fragments of old pine forest. More woodland is more room for them.

Pip Gullett of Cairngorms Connect, a co-author, said the method is also good at tracking the effects of fires, which are growing more severe with climate change.

Field crews from the partnership and RSPB Scotland had already surveyed parts of the landscape on foot. The laser count of land with more than 100 trees per hectare came out in the same range as those ground estimates once a correction was applied.

Field crews who measured saplings a year later found them slightly taller than the laser had. A batch of 136 Scots pines averaging 7 feet (2.1 meters) tall had grown about 7 inches (17.6 centimeters) in that year. Seedlings still below the heather line remain uncounted.

Rocks and clumps of bracken can be mistaken for trees, and the authors filtered them out using color images taken on the same flight. The method has only been tested at this one site, with this one scanner and flight height.

The Scottish Government is now commissioning a laser scan of the whole country. The authors wrote that their approach could be scaled up to build a national record of woodland expansion.

Chan said the next thing he wants to map is the shrub layer itself. Dozens of species depend on the heather and blaeberry, he said, and that layer sets much of the fire risk.

Until that map exists, the count stops at the trees tall enough to clear the heather.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Applied Ecology.

#6392. Gut bacteria plays a huge role in vaccine side effects

Gut bacteria that make a protein called flagellin keep low-grade inflammation going, and the people carrying more of them ran a fever.

For some people, a COVID shot means a night of chills and a headache. Others barely notice theirs, and the split holds, dose after dose. To some, this has always looked like luck.

Researchers have now found part of the reason, and it was in the gut before the needle went in. Certain bacteria there build whip-like tails out of a protein that the immune system reads as a warning.

People whose gut bacteria made more of that protein were the ones who ran a fever.

Kelsey Huus and her colleagues at the Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen followed 171 healthy adults in Germany through an mRNA vaccination against SARS-CoV-2.

In people they can only show that gut microbes and fever go together, so they tested cause in mice and in human gut cells grown in a dish.

If gut bacteria set the risk of a fever, that risk may be something a person can change, though that has not been shown in people.

In an interview with Earth.com, Ruth Ley, the study’s senior author, said the bigger idea isn’t really about vaccines at all.

“More broadly, I think the interesting idea coming from the study is that the gut microbiome helps set our baseline inflammatory ‘immune tone,'” she said. “That could potentially be relevant well beyond vaccination.”

Participants took their own temperature three times a day for two weeks, before and after their shot, and wrote every reading in a diary. The diaries came to 7,079 readings from 171 people.

The median was 97.7°F (36.5°C), which is below the 98.6°F (37°C) most of us were taught to expect.

Instead of using a clinical cutoff, the team compared each person against their own normal for that hour of the day.

Anyone whose temperature climbed 1.4°F (0.8°C) or more above their own baseline counted as fever-high. That line left 72 people above it and 99 below.

People who said earlier doses had given them a fever ran hot here too. The two groups also differed on a stool test for gut inflammation. This was higher in the fever-high group two weeks after the shot and tilted the same way beforehand.

Many gut bacteria grow whip-like tails to move around. Those tails are built from a protein the immune system treats as a sign that bacteria are on the move. The protein is called flagellin.

The team read the RNA in each stool sample to see which bacterial genes were switched on. In the fever-high group the flagellin genes were running harder, before the vaccine as well as after. Those gut microbiomes carried a wider variety of flagellins to start with.

One genus accounted for most of that. Waltera, a member of the Lachnospiraceae family, made 67.2 percent of the flagellins that were more active in fever-high people. The family as a whole made 76.3 percent.

That genus was also the only one reliably more common in the fever-high group.

The same thing turned up in a second group of people. Among 1,014 Canadian adults in the CHILD Cohort Study who answered questions about side effects after a SARS-CoV-2 vaccine, the ones who reported any had more Waltera in their stool.

Measuring flagellin isn’t the same as showing it does something, so the team ran two experiments.

First they grew human colon cells in a dish and bathed them in stool extracts from the participants. Extracts from fever-high people pushed those cells to release more of an inflammatory signal, and the amount tracked how much active flagellin each sample held.

Then they transplanted human microbiomes into germ-free mice and vaccinated them. A mouse with an inflammatory reaction doesn’t run a fever. Its temperature drops instead.

Mice carrying a fever-high person’s gut bacteria dropped further, and how far they dropped tracked the fever that person had run.

Mice bred without the two receptors that detect flagellin still reacted, though less, so flagellin carries part of the signal and something else carries the rest.

The animal work was done at Georgia State University, and the gut cells and the additive cultures were handled with Institut Pasteur in Paris.

Diet changed the same thing. In culture, the common thickener carboxymethylcellulose helped Waltera grow, and raised the amount of inflammatory flagellin it made.

In tanks seeded with stool from two donors, that thickener on its own barely shifted those bacteria. A mix of it and 13 other additives of the kind that go into ultra-processed foods raised both the bacteria and the flagellin they made.

Mice fed a Western-style diet, high in fat and low in fiber, reacted harder to the vaccine than mice on standard chow. Their temperatures dropped further, and a day later they carried more of a second inflammatory signal.

Among the 171 people, 46 said they ate a plant-based diet. Temperatures rose less in that group than in the 125 omnivores.

The gap held even after the team adjusted for gender, age, body mass index, dose, fever medication, earlier fevers and starting antibody levels.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most, Ley pointed at how fast diet changed what the bacteria produced in the laboratory. “That gives us a plausible way in which diet could influence inflammatory immune tone through the microbiome,” she said.

None of this reached the part of the vaccine response that protects you. Fever-high participants carried somewhat higher antibody levels before and after their shot, but the booster lifted both groups by the same amount,. Diet made no difference either.

The mice ended up in the same place. Germ-free animals given fever-high or fever-low microbiomes finished with matching antibody levels, and the ones that cannot detect flagellin made antibodies anyway.

“This suggests that the mechanisms that make someone feel ill after vaccination are at least partly distinct from those responsible for generating protective antibodies,” Ley told Earth.com.

The human diet data are the thinnest part of the work. Participants picked from broad categories rather than filling in a food diary, and Ley said as much herself.

“But the dietary findings in people are much more preliminary: we only have broad, self-reported dietary categories, so we cannot conclude that diet caused the differences in fever that we observed,” she said.

The group was narrow by design. Everyone was a healthy adult between 18 and 40, with a median age of 25 years. Anyone immunocompromised, living with a gut disorder or recently on antibiotics was left out.

Huus and her co-authors wrote that their definitions of fever were built for research and may not meet the standard for a clinical diagnosis.

Ley said she wants to know first whether the same pattern shows up in other groups of people.

“One important next step is to determine whether the relationship between microbial flagellin and vaccine reactions holds across different populations, age groups and vaccines,” she said.

Her team also wants to know whether a person’s inflammatory tone can be shifted at all, which would take a controlled diet trial.

For now, a fever after a shot may say as much about the gut it arrives in as about the shot itself.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6391. The saying ‘blind as a bat’ is completely wrong, according to a new study

New research shows that bats have tiny eyes to stabilize vision and combine sight with echolocation to navigate and hunt.

Bats are not blind. They have small eyes with very sensitive vision that lets them see in conditions people might call pitch black, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).

Their eyesight is not as sharp or as colorful as ours, but it does not need to be. The agency likens bat vision to that of “a dark-adapted Mr. Magoo,” the cartoon character known for his poor eyesight.

Recent studies show how much bats use that vision. A 2026 study from Johns Hopkins University found that bats move their eyes to steady their view, overturning an assumption that dates to 1942.

Optometrist Gordon Walls made the claim in his 1942 book The Vertebrate Eye and Its Adaptive Radiation. He wrote that the eyes of small nocturnal mammals, bats among them, “never move even reflexively.”

The idea went untested for more than 80 years. It fit a view of bats as animals that rely on echolocation for nearly all of their navigation.

Kathleen Cullen is the Raj and Neera Singh Professor of Biomedical Engineering at Johns Hopkins. Her team tested the assumption in Seba’s short-tailed bats, Carollia perspicillata.

The team included Grace Capshaw, Dimitri Skandalis and Cynthia F. Moss of Johns Hopkins, along with Hui Ho Vanessa Chang of Inha University. Chang carried out the work as a Ph.D. student in Cullen’s lab.

The researchers moved visual patterns in front of the bats and recorded the animals’ eye responses.

The bats tracked the moving patterns across a range of about 10 degrees in each direction. The eyes slowly followed the motion, then quickly snapped back to center.

That response, called the optokinetic reflex, helps keep an image steady on the retina. It resembled the response of mice and other mammals.

The team also passively rotated the bats’ heads from side to side. Unlike in most mammals, their eyes barely moved in response to that rotation.

The bats did show strong eye responses driven by the otolith organs, which sense gravity and linear motion, when rotated on a tilted axis.

Micro-CT scans showed that their inner-ear balance organs are nearly identical to those of mice, which responded strongly to head rotation. The difference appears to lie in how the brain uses those signals.

The authors propose that the system is specialized for active flight. It stays relatively quiet when a bat is at rest but likely engages during rapid, acrobatic maneuvers.

The eye-movement experiments compared four bats with six mice.

“This study shows that the brain’s solutions to navigation are more flexible than we assumed,” Cullen said.

“Even in an animal as specialized as the bat, multiple senses are integrated in ways that depend on behavior and environment,” she added.

“In bats, we see that this integration is dynamically tuned depending on context,” she explained. “The same is true for humans.”

Understanding how the brain combines these senses could help in treating balance disorders and in designing better rehabilitation and assistive technologies, according to Cullen.

A 2025 study of wild common noctules, Nyctalus noctula, showed vision at work during hunting. Researchers from the Leibniz Institute for Zoo and Wildlife Research (Leibniz-IZW) and Aarhus University tagged 21 bats with miniature sensors.

The tags recorded light levels, echolocation calls and movements. When the bats hunted in brighter conditions, they cut their calling rate in half and called up to 7 decibels louder.

They also flapped harder and flew faster. Average foraging speed rose from about 11.6 mph (5.2 meters per second) in the dark to about 17.7 mph (7.9 meters per second) in light.

Prey capture was about 50 percent faster in lit conditions. When the bats were simply commuting, their calls and flight did not change with brightness.

Laura Stidsholt, the study’s first author, was a postdoctoral researcher at the Leibniz-IZW and is now at Aarhus University.

“We show that the bats reduce the acoustic tracking of their prey when enough light is available as complementary sensory information,” Stidsholt said.

Calling less did not make the bats worse hunters. “At the same time, we were able to reveal that this happens not at the expense of hunting efficiency,” Stidsholt pointed out.

Insect-eating bats are very active in the early hours of the night, at dusk. They can presumably combine echolocation and vision most efficiently then, in the view of Christian Voigt, head of the Leibniz-IZW Department of Evolutionary Ecology.

“Our study provides the first direct evidence that bats rely on multisensory information when foraging, highlighting the remarkable flexibility of their sensory systems,” Voigt noted.

The Johns Hopkins team reaches a similar conclusion. Its results challenge the view that bats rely almost entirely on sound, showing instead that they combine vision and sonar to make split-second decisions.

The study was published in the journal Current Biology.

In a key coastal area of Peru, violence was low despite the practice of human sacrifice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite engaging in human sacrifice, the people who lived in the Lambayeque Valley of northern Peru had low levels of violence, a new study of their remains finds.

Human sacrifice occurred in the valley over the millennia. It's thought that at least some of these mass sacrifices were attempts to appease the gods in the wake of El Niño, a periodic weather phenomenon that can lead to intense rains and flooding in Peru and droughts in other parts of South and Central America.

"We have one example at the site of Sicán where around [A.D.] 1050/1100, around 200 individuals were killed and ritualistically buried during an intense El Niño event," study co-author Haagen Klaus, an anthropology professor at George Mason University in Virginia, told Live Science in an email.

Other human sacrifice findings include more than 200 children found near the modern-day town of Huanchaco who were sacrificed sometime between 600 and 800 years ago, possibly during an El Niño.

However, despite the occurrence of human sacrifice, levels of violence unrelated to sacrifice were actually quite low in the Lambayeque Valley. In the study, scientists analyzed the skeletal remains of 1,519 people from the Lambayeque Valley who lived between roughly 1500 B.C. and A.D. 1800, and whose remains were preserved enough to detect signs of violent trauma, including interpersonal violence.

A skull showing blunt force trauma that dates to the Chimu period, roughly 1375 to 1490.

Of these skeletons, "only 25 (1.6%) exhibited traumatic lesions consistent with interpersonal conflict, and 77 exhibited post-cranial traumatic lesions consistent with accidental trauma (5.1%)," Klaus and co-author Thomas Snyder, a bioarchaeologist at New York University, wrote in the paper, which was published Nov. 8 in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The team didn't find any link between a person's sex and violence, they noted. The findings mean that despite the presence of human sacrifice, the amount of violence unrelated to sacrifice was low. This leaves a question: Why?

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A healed fracture on the left leg of a person who lived sometime between 1000 to 650 B.C. The fracture may have been from an accident.

"Ritual violence may have alleviated non-ritual violence by creating spaces where social tensions could get worked out in a few different ways," Klaus said.

It's important to remember that other areas of Peru also practiced human sacrifice but didn't have the same low levels of interpersonal violence. Klaus noted that areas in the Peruvian highlands sometimes had higher rates of interpersonal violence. In their paper, Klaus and Snyder noted that societies that originated in the highlands, such as the Tiwanaku, Wari and Inca had to grapple with poorer soils and cold temperatures, and these challenges may have been a factor in increasing the levels of interpersonal violence.

The "evidence of sub-lethal and lethal violence forceful enough to break bone is significantly higher in some areas of Peru's highlands," Klaus said. He and Snyder noted in their paper that the inhabitants of the Lambayeque Valley may have had better access to marine and water resources, such as seafood and rivers that could be used for agricultural irrigation, than those who lived in highland areas. Access to these resources may have helped alleviate interpersonal violence in the valley by providing more food resources, they wrote.

Aside from practicing human sacrifice, people in the valley may have engaged in other practices that helped lower levels of interpersonal violence, researchers who were not involved in the new study told Live Science.

Environmental conditions may have helped reduce conflict or there could be "really unusual cultural practices in this region of avoiding or mediating conflict — both between and within groups," Elizabeth Arkush, an anthropology professor at the University of Pittsburgh, said in an email.

Constanza Ceruti, an anthropologist and explorer with the National Geographic Society, said in an email that she's glad that researchers are studying human sacrifices "after decades of being ignored as a taboo topic in academic discussion." She praised the study’s large sample size and noted that human sacrifice is a "phenomenon primarily associated [with] the manipulation and concentration of power by elites."

Jordi Rivera Prince, an anthropology professor at Tulane University, said that the findings dovetail with her excavations in the region, where she has "found little evidence of violent trauma during the Salinar (400-200 BCE), a period of great social change in the Andes."

Weston McCool, an archaeology professor at Cal Poly, said in an email that the newly published paper "is an interesting study that provides additional evidence for a sharp break in patterns of violence between the Andean coast and highlands." He noted that it "supports the hypothesis that coastal populations were buffered from terrestrial environmental downturns in ways that highland populations were not. The nature of that resilience, however, remains an important question for future research."

Snyder, T. J., & Klaus, H. D. (2026). Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, 5, 1889466. https://doi.org/10.3389/fearc.2026.1889466

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6388. Memory tests may miss clues hidden in the time it takes to answer

Memory tests may reveal more than correct answers, as slower responses in older adults could signal subtle changes.

Getting an answer right on a memory test is usually considered a good sign. But what if it takes someone much longer to reach that answer?

That delay might tell us something important.

New research suggests that the time older adults take to answer memory questions could reveal subtle changes in how their brains work, even when they manage to give the right answers.

Anglia Ruskin University researchers found that older adults with possible mild cognitive impairment (MCI) answered some memory questions more slowly than healthy older adults. Distractions made the gap clearer.

MCI affects memory and thinking beyond normal aging, but people can usually manage daily life. Some later develop dementia, though many do not.

Professor Shahina Pardhan, who worked on the study, thinks measuring answer times alongside memory scores could help doctors spot early changes. The idea needs more testing.

The study brought together 115 people. There were 34 young adults, aged 18 to 30, and 61 healthy older adults, aged 55 or above.

Another 20 older adults had scored below the cutoff on at least one of two standard screening tests. The team placed them in an at-risk group for mild cognitive impairment, or MCI.

Nobody in that group had a confirmed MCI diagnosis. Those screening results were a reason to investigate, rather than proof that someone had the condition.

People with MCI have more difficulty with memory and thinking than normal aging would explain, but can usually get on with everyday activities. Some later develop dementia, though many do not.

In the word task, people watched two or four color words appear briefly in different places. The computer then showed one again and asked whether it was in the place where they’d seen it before.

Participants had to remember each word’s location while ignoring its ink color.

A mismatch between a color word and its ink, such as “red” printed in blue, can create interference known as the Stroop effect.

The at-risk group got more answers wrong than both the young and healthy older groups.

With two words to remember, they took longer to answer too; the timing differences between groups weren’t clear enough to rule out chance with four words.

There was no instruction to hurry. Participants were asked to get the answers right, while the computer recorded how long each response took.

In the arrow task, an arrow could point in one direction while moving in another. For example, it might point left and move right, or point and move in the same direction.

At the time they saw an arrow, participants didn’t know what they’d be asked to recall about it.

Either its movement or the way it pointed could come up in the question, so they had to remember both.

It wasn’t possible to pick one detail and ignore the other throughout the task, as they could with ink color.

Remembering both might have changed how they dealt with a mismatch, the researchers suggested.

With two arrows to remember or four, the at-risk group answered more slowly than healthy older adults.

But unlike the two other groups, they showed no clear extra delay when an arrow’s movement and pointing direction clashed.

Healthy older adults did about as well as young adults with the words, but made more mistakes with the arrows. The two groups answered at similar speeds on the arrow task despite that difference in mistakes.

For young adults and healthy older adults, wrong answers on the word test generally took longer than correct ones.

Perhaps they hesitated because they weren’t sure, the researchers suggested.

The 20 at-risk participants took roughly the same time whether they were right or wrong. One possibility is that they were less aware of making mistakes, though the study didn’t establish this.

And that pattern didn’t carry over to the arrows. All three groups took longer when they gave a wrong answer on that task.

For both older groups, words in matching ink were quicker to deal with than words in clashing ink. Young adults showed little measurable change between those conditions.

The at-risk participants were slowest of all on the conflicting word trials.

They were also slower than healthy older adults on the arrows overall, so the lack of an extra delay from mismatched arrows wasn’t evidence of better performance.

Answers to the word task weren’t clearly less accurate when the ink clashed.

That’s something an accuracy score alone could miss: people could still choose correctly, while needing more time to do it.

The researchers suggested that ignoring the ink took extra effort.

Age can make it harder to keep unwanted information out, and memory and thinking problems may add to that difficulty.

Researchers tested participants once, so they couldn’t link slower answers to later memory loss or MCI. The at-risk group included only 20 people, none with a confirmed MCI diagnosis.

The reasons for the delays remain unclear, and the lab tasks may not reflect everyday memory.

Larger studies following people over time, including adults with diagnosed MCI, could help test the approach.

Professor Shahina Pardhan, who worked on the study, sees promise in measuring response times.

“These findings suggest that measuring reaction times alongside memory performance could help clinicians detect subtle cognitive changes at an earlier stage,” Pardhan said.

“As populations continue to age and dementia becomes an increasing public health challenge, there is a growing need for sensitive, accessible tools that can identify people at greater risk before symptoms become more severe.”

The full study was published in the journal Brain Sciences.
