#6387. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

K. Grice et al. Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2026. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2614248123

D.M. Martill and D.M. Unwin. Small spheres in fossil bones: Blood corpuscles or diagenetic products? Palaeontology. 1997.

#6386. AI can copy how people write online, but one thing still gives it away

Nine AI models learned the shape of online replies in a new test, but AI-generated text still gave itself away through emotion and tone.

Ask a chatbot to write a reply to a post the way a regular person would, and the result usually reads fine. That is the problem. A reply can sound natural to a human reader and still be nothing like what a real person would have written.

A computer program, however, told the two apart 70 to 80 percent of the time.

Nicolò Pagan of the University of Zurich and Petter Törnberg of the University of Amsterdam ran that test on nine AI language models. The raw material was real conversations from X, Bluesky, and Reddit.

The models learned the shape of online talk well enough. What they couldn’t fake was the feeling behind it, and the harder the team pushed them to sound human, the less they said what the human had actually said.

The stakes go beyond spotting bots. Social scientists have started using these models as stand-ins for people, simulating how crowds might react to a news feed or a policy.

The study asks whether the stand-ins behave like the people they replace.

The team collected replies that real users had posted to real messages. The sample held 275 users on X, 492 on Reddit’s politics forum, and 59 groups of similar accounts on Bluesky, with 20 replies each.

Then they asked each AI model to write its own reply to the same original message, in the style of the same user.

A separate program was trained to look at a reply and guess whether a person or a model wrote it. If the AI replies were indistinguishable from the human ones, that guess would be right about half the time, no better than a coin toss.

The nine models came from six families, including Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and DeepSeek. Most were small by today’s standards, and one, Llama 3.1 70B, was far larger.

All were open-weight models that researchers can run on their own computers, so the biggest commercial chatbots, such as ChatGPT, were not tested.

Christopher Bail of Duke University and Christopher Barrie of New York University and the University of Oxford were co-authors on the research publication.

The standard setup feeds the model a written description of the user’s personality and interests. With that alone, the detector was right at least 87 percent of the time for every model on every platform.

The clearest tells were how long the replies ran, how long the words were, and how toxic the language was. The models wrote longer replies than people did, and the versions tuned to be helpful assistants produced less hostile language than real users.

Several models also stuffed replies with hashtags and mentions that real users almost never used.

On the emotional side, the replies differed from human ones in categories such as positive emotion, negative emotion, and the language of speaking and communicating.

In an interview with Earth.com, Törnberg said the most surprising part was how stubborn those gaps were. “What surprised me most was how persistent the differences were,” he said.

“So in a sense, the models can become quite good at reproducing the form of online conversation, but less so with its feeling.”

The team tried five ways of coaching the models, each one adding to the last.

These were a bare prompt, a prompt with a persona description, ten examples of the user’s past replies, relevant snippets pulled from the user’s history and, finally, retraining the model itself on the user’s writing.

The persona description, which is how most researchers currently do this, made little difference and sometimes made the replies easier to spot. Retraining was unpredictable, and for several models it made detection easier.

The two simplest moves worked best. Showing the model ten real examples cut the detector’s accuracy between about 2 and 10 percent. Adding the user’s past context cut another 2 to 3 percent.

Even the best combinations left the detector right 70 to 80 percent of the time. The bigger model was no better at passing than the small ones, and models tuned to be helpful assistants were generally worse than their raw counterparts.

“I would not assume that newer models will necessarily be better models of human behavior,” Törnberg told Earth.com. He said the training that makes a model helpful and well behaved may be the same training that makes its language less like real human communication.

The study’s second measure asked whether the AI-generated text meant the same thing as the reply the human actually wrote. The team scored that by converting both replies into numbers that capture meaning and comparing them.

The coaching that made replies harder to detect also moved them slightly further from the human reply’s meaning on every platform. The models were learning to write like a person in general, not to say what that person would say.

Next, each model wrote 20 candidate replies, and the team picked one in two ways. Choosing the reply that best matched the human’s meaning roughly doubled the similarity score but did not reliably make the reply harder to detect.

Choosing the reply most likely to fool the detector trimmed its accuracy by 5 to 10 points but left the meaning no closer. The two methods picked the same reply only 5 to 10 percent of the time, about what chance would give.

Asked by Earth.com what else stood out, Törnberg pointed to that trade-off. The team could make replies harder to tell from human writing, he said, but doing so often made them less similar in meaning to what the real person wrote.

Every message in the dataset had only one real human reply, so the meaning score measured closeness to that one reply, not whether the AI’s reply was a reasonable one.

On X, the comparison between two humans answering the same post rested on only 18 pairs, which the authors treated as exploratory.

The models also saw less of each conversation than the human replying had seen. And the detector was more likely to flag a real person as a bot than to miss a bot.

Whether future models close the gap is an open question, the authors wrote, and their test is built to keep asking it. Even a model that passed every statistical check, they added, would not necessarily hold the attitudes behind a human reply.

Törnberg said the fix for researchers is to validate a simulation against real human behavior in the specific setting being studied, rather than trust that it sounds right.

And getting the feeling right, the authors wrote, may take new training goals that target emotional expression directly instead of copying style.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6385. Even remote wildlife can’t escape microplastics in their blood

Scientists found microplastics in the blood of wild tapirs and giant anteaters in Brazil, including animals living far from human development.

As the afternoon sun began to fade over Brazil’s countryside, a team of researchers drove along dusty dirt roads searching for giant anteaters.

Two spotters rode in the back of the truck, scanning the landscape for signs of movement. When they spotted an anteater, the team approached on foot with two long-handled nets.

Capturing the animal usually took about a minute, but the information gathered would help answer a much bigger question: How far has plastic pollution spread into the natural world?

The researchers were investigating whether wild animals living closer to human activity had more microplastics in their blood.

Their findings revealed a clear connection between human disturbance and plastic exposure.

But one discovery was particularly concerning.

Even in Brazil’s remote Pantanal, the world’s largest tropical wetland, every animal sampled had microplastics in its blood, despite living more than 40 miles (65 kilometers) from the nearest development.

The results suggest that plastic pollution is reaching wildlife even in places that appear largely untouched by humans.

Scientists had widely assumed a connection between human activity and plastic in wildlife.

To test it, the researchers needed several records for the same animals, namely blood samples, GPS movements and detailed maps of human disturbance.

Study co-author Justin Calabrese of the Center for Advanced Systems Understanding (CASUS) described the difficulty of getting all those records together.

“Such integrated datasets simply did not exist,” Calabrese said.

Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz and Michael Noonan, both at the University of British Columbia Okanagan, conceived the study.

Teams from two long-running conservation programs in Brazil did the fieldwork.

From February 2021 to November 2022, those teams collected blood from 26 lowland tapirs and 21 giant anteaters.

The animals lived at a soy farm on the Amazon’s deforestation frontier, farmland in the Cerrado savanna and a cattle ranch in the Pantanal.

For the anteaters, the work took place near two federal highways, where the Anteaters and Highways Project studies collisions between vehicles and wildlife.

Each blood sample went into a glass tube, which the field team sealed with aluminum foil to prevent contamination.

To record where the animals went, adult tapirs wore GPS collars that logged an hourly position. The anteaters wore GPS trackers as well.

Once in the lab, each sample went through a chemical treatment to break down the blood. The team collected the solids left behind on a filter.

Raman spectroscopy then identified the materials from the way they scattered light from a laser.

When the team had checked all 47 blood samples, 43 contained microplastics. The particles averaged about 0.0004 inches (10 micrometers) in length.

Pieces of that size need a microscope to be seen.

Counts for individual animals ran from zero to more than 1,200 particles in a milliliter of blood. The average for all the animals was about 74, and a milliliter is roughly a fifth of a teaspoon.

For comparison, the average fell within the range already reported in human blood by other studies using spectroscopy.

The tapirs had about 99 particles per milliliter on average and the anteaters about 43. The difference between the species was not statistically significant.

GPS records provided more than 440,000 locations, allowing researchers to map the home ranges of 40 animals.

To describe the land within those areas the researchers used the Human Footprint Index.

This global map has scores running from zero for undisturbed land up to 50 for the most heavily modified.

An animal did not need to live across uniformly disturbed land for a link to appear.

The team found more particles in blood when the most heavily modified spot in an animal’s range had a higher footprint score.

Average footprint scores across entire home ranges were not significantly associated with microplastic levels.

The distance comparisons also pointed to less plastic in animals living farther from development, which here meant urban areas, mines and power plants.

The same was true of animals living farther from waste management facilities.

Calabrese said the paper “is the first to demonstrate this linkage for terrestrial mammals,” meaning mammals that live on land.

The researchers also checked how much the highest values influenced the findings. They ran each test again without the animals making up the top 10% for that measure.

For the distance tests, that meant leaving out the animals living farthest away.

After that check the footprint link remained, while neither distance link was still statistically significant.

Animals with more farmland in their home ranges did not have higher microplastic levels in their blood.

The authors suggested that farmland may add less direct exposure to microplastics than other kinds of human disturbance.

The types of plastic offered another comparison between sites, with differences the authors described as consistent with local land use.

Animals at the Amazon farm carried more polyamide, the main material in fishing nets and ropes, than animals on Cerrado farmland.

The Cerrado animals had more PVC, a material used in irrigation pipes, than animals in the Pantanal.

The authors described the site comparisons as case studies, with uneven numbers of animals at each site.

For the animals at the cattle ranch in the Pantanal, the distance from the nearest waste facility was about 70 miles (112 kilometers). Each of them still carried microplastics in its blood.

The researchers also obtained a value of about 10 particles per milliliter of blood from their model for land with a footprint score of zero.

The authors suggested that the value may partly reflect limitations of the model.

Even so, they wrote that direct contact with land changed by people was unlikely to be the only route into wildlife.

The authors identified wind and water as likely routes carrying microplastics into remote habitats. Cities, industry and farms supply airborne microplastics that may settle far away.

Runoff, rivers and seasonal floods provide ways for particles to move far from their sources as well.

Microplastics in the water and sediment of the Pantanal were already known from previous studies.

The highest measurements in those studies came from places near rivers flowing out of urban areas.

This observational study found associations between human disturbance and microplastic levels in blood, but it cannot establish cause and effect.

The researchers had a single blood sample from each animal. Their method could not identify particles smaller than about 0.00004 inches (one micrometer).

Future studies could collect blood, soil and water samples from the same locations to help trace the particles’ sources.

The team did not collect those environmental samples and could not yet match the plastic in blood to its source.

The measurements also concern the amount of plastic, without examining its effects on the health of these wild animals. Laboratory experiments have shown that microplastics can harm animals.

For the years 2001 to 2020, the increase in Brazil’s average footprint score was 42%, whereas the worldwide increase was 26%.

Thus, as land development continues, the authors suggested that the plastic levels in land animals would continue to increase.

They described keeping wildlife farther from development and waste facilities as a possible way to lower the amount the animals carry.

The study is published in the journal Nature.

A DNA analysis has confirmed that a Nazca infant who lived in southern Peru 1,600 years ago had a rare congenital condition called trisomy 13.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Peru have discovered the skeleton of an infant with a rare birth defect that left only one central eye socket in the child's skull. DNA analysis of the remains confirmed a chromosomal abnormality caused the deadly condition in the infant over 1,600 years ago, according to a new study.

"We cannot really say how long this individual survived," study co-author Lars Fehren-Schmitz, an anthropologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told Live Science in an email. But "the burial of this infant suggests that the Nasca treated this individual in death like most other infants."

The skeleton of this female infant was discovered alongside a second one inside a ceramic urn at the archaeological site of Jauranga in Peru's Palpa Valley, where numerous geoglyphs known as the Nazca Lines have been found. Archaeologists uncovered several dozen other burials dated to the Middle Nazca (also spelled Nasca) period (A.D. 325 to 440) at the site, but one of the co-buried infants had an extremely rare condition, researchers wrote in a study published Monday (Nov. 9) in the journal PNAS.

The infant had a very small skull and a single eye socket in the middle of her face, along with other developmental issues of the cranial bones. These traits match modern clinical descriptions of cyclopia, a lethal condition that occurs when the front part of a fetus's brain fails to divide into left and right hemispheres.

This condition can also cause alterations in the nasal structures, resulting in a missing nose or a tube-like nose above the single eye.

A medical illustration from 1891 of two infants with cyclopia.

"The cause of the malformation was present at fertilization, but manifestation occurs around the fourth to fifth week in utero [in the womb], when the frontal lobe of the brain has to divide," study first author Elsa Tomasto-Cagigao, an archaeologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told Live Science in an email.

Cyclopia is a rare condition, occurring in about 1 out of every 100,000 births. To learn more about the infant's short life, the researchers sequenced her genome. (DNA suggested the infant carried two X chromosomes, typical of a female.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team detected an extra copy of chromosome 13, meaning the infant had a genetic condition called trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome. It's known to be a major chromosomal cause of cyclopia; that said, only a small percentage of trisomy 13 cases involve cyclopia.

While trisomy 13 is associated with advanced maternal age, it is not clear whether that was the case for this infant, Fehren-Schmitz said.

"This condition has been documented in historic and modern anatomical collections, but to my knowledge this is the first archaeological example of this developmental abnormality," Siân Halcrow, a bioarchaeologist at Durham University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

The researchers' estimate of the infant's age at death suggests she may have survived for several weeks or months after birth, Halcrow pointed out. "This raises important questions about how infants with profound congenital differences were cared for and treated in past societies," she said.

The infant was buried in a ceramic urn, the researchers noted in the study, which was a common burial method in the Nazca period, along with a second female infant who had no skeletal abnormalities. "The baby with cyclopia was at the bottom of the jar, while the other baby was on top. Nevertheless, it appears that they were interred in a single event," Tomasto-Cagigao said. The genetic analysis showed that the two infants did not have the same mother.

A burial of two infants in one urn is unusual for this culture, the researchers said, but there is not enough archaeological evidence to conclude that the infant with cyclopia was given a different type of burial.

"The fact that the individual was buried with a 'healthy' individual in a regular cemetery, without any special grave goods, suggests that, to some extent, the individual was not treated differently in death, even though it had such a rare condition," Fehren-Schmitz said. "It was neither 'excluded' because of it nor treated in a 'special' way."

In ancient Andean societies, some people with disabilities took on special societal roles, such as ones associated with religious practices. "If that reflects Nasca society as a whole, we can't say based on one case," Fehren-Schmitz said, "but it does reflect the community this infant was part of, even if only briefly."

Tomasto-Cagigao, E., Reindel, M., Isla Cuadrado, J., Lund Valle, M., Kassadjikova, K., Harkins, K., Fehren-Schmitz, L. (2026). A Nasca-period perinatal burial reveals cyclopia associated with trisomy 13 in southern Peru. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.2625042123

#6382. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

#6381. Dancing may shape how the brain responds to other people’s emotions

Ballet dancers show different brain responses to emotional faces, without identifying emotions more accurately than people without training.

Ballet dancers spend years training their bodies to move with precision.

A new study suggests that the same training is also linked to how the brain responds when a dancer sees fear or happiness on someone’s face.

When ballet dancers looked at photos of fearful, happy, and neutral faces, their brain activity differed from that of people with no dance training.

The differences appeared in brain areas that process vision and in areas that process touch.

Beatriz Calvo-Merino worked with lead author Vasiliki Meletaki and Bettina Forster at City St George’s, University of London’s Centre for Cognition and Neuroscience.

“The impact of dance expertise goes beyond movement and taps into social perception mechanisms, such as face processing and emotions,” said Calvo-Merino.

The team compared 26 professional or trainee ballet dancers with 26 people of similar age and sex who had no dance experience.

The dancers had been dancing for about 17 years on average.

Both groups judged the emotions about equally well, but their brain signals differed in timing and pattern.

Earlier brain-scanning studies, including work by Calvo-Merino, found increased activity in the brains of expert dancers when they watched familiar dance movements.

Nearly all of that research looked at how dancers perceive movement and bodies, the authors wrote.

The team used faces to test whether dancers’ brains also differ in other, everyday kinds of perception.

The test is based on an idea about emotion.

According to this idea, people perceive someone else’s emotion partly through their own body’s sense of that emotion, and not through vision alone.

Researchers describe this as an embodied view of emotion.

Earlier experiments found that the brain area receiving touch and movement signals from the body is involved when people look at emotional faces. That area is the somatosensory cortex.

Professional dancers develop a refined awareness of their own bodies through long, precise training, the authors wrote.

Dance training might also refine the body’s part in perceiving emotion, the team reasoned. If so, dancers’ brains should respond differently to emotional faces as well as to dance.

Each volunteer wore a cap fitted with 64 electrodes. The electrodes recorded the brain’s electrical activity, a method called EEG.

The faces came from a photo collection called the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces. The team used 60 black-and-white photos, half of them male faces.

Each face stayed on screen for 600 milliseconds, a little over half a second.

In one task, a question about emotion sometimes followed a face, such as “Is s/he fearful?” In the other task, used as a comparison, the question asked whether the face was male or female.

Half of the time, a blunt-tipped device gave a brief touch to the tip of the volunteer’s left index finger.

The touch came 105 milliseconds after a face appeared, and volunteers were told to ignore it.

The touch served as a probe. The team recorded the brain’s response to a face with a touch and to a face alone, then subtracted the second recording from the first.

The subtraction helped isolate the brain’s response to touch. Differences between facial expressions could then indicate that emotional processing was influencing that response.

In the dancers, the touch response differed between fearful and neutral faces at the earliest stage the team analyzed.

That stage was about 143 to 173 milliseconds after the face appeared, less than a fifth of a second.

The response to happy faces didn’t differ from the response to neutral faces at that stage. The early effect was specific to fearful expressions, the authors wrote.

In non-dancers, the touch response didn’t differ by emotion at that first stage.

Their touch responses did differ by emotion at later stages, but at a narrower set of recording sites than in dancers.

“What is particularly interesting is that dance expertise appears to influence how the somatosensory cortex responds to emotions expressed by others,” Forster said.

“This suggests that our own bodily experiences can shape how the brain processes other people’s emotions, providing further evidence for the embodied nature of emotion perception.”

Electrodes over the visual areas at the back of the head recorded a second set of differences.

One difference appeared between about 150 and 200 milliseconds after a face came on screen. In dancers, visual responses to neutral faces differed from responses to both fearful and happy faces.

In non-dancers, visual responses at that stage were different for each of the three expressions. Those differences were also stronger on the right side of the brain, a pattern that earlier face studies have typically reported.

In dancers, the differences were spread across both sides. The authors called the two patterns distinct styles of telling emotions apart.

Both groups processed fearful faces in a distinct way. The authors linked that result to the priority the brain is known to give fear.

The authors also wrote, as an anecdote, that fear is an important tool in dance training. Dancers learn to feel comfortable performing in front of an audience, for example.

The study found no clear advantage in dancers’ ability to identify facial emotions.

During the recordings, dancers answered 94% of the emotion questions correctly. Non-dancers answered 95% of them correctly, a gap too small to rule out chance.

Dancers did score higher on a questionnaire about awareness of signals from inside the body. Their average score was 3.69, compared with 2.71 for non-dancers.

Body awareness may be part of how dancers process other people’s emotions, the authors suggested. They proposed exploring that relationship further.

Each group had 26 people, a size chosen to match earlier studies. The authors sugg that future studies should calculate in advance how many participants they need.

Scalp recordings also couldn’t show precisely where in the brain the differing touch responses arose.

The study compared the two groups at a single point in time, so it can’t show how the differences developed.

The next question is whether the brain differences are accompanied by differences in behavior.

Future studies could add behavioral tests of emotion recognition, the authors wrote.

New studies could also explore how the touch area’s response to emotion changes across stages of dance training, from advanced trainees to professional performers.

The full study was published in the journal Cerebral Cortex.

#6379. Could a nuclear blast save Earth from an asteroid? Good aim will mean everything

Computer simulations reveal how an asteroid’s shape could affect efforts to push it off course with X-rays from a nearby nuclear blast.

A nuclear blast set off near a dangerous asteroid could, in theory, push it away from Earth. But if the asteroid has a lumpy, uneven shape, how hard it gets pushed depends on which side the blast hits.

In new computer tests, hitting one side of an oddly shaped asteroid instead of another gave it nearly five times as much push.

So a real defense mission could depend on knowing an asteroid’s shape before anyone chooses where to aim.

Nathan Moore, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories, led the research. “We expected aim to matter,” he said. “What surprised us was how much.”

No asteroid was blasted for this work. The team ran every test in computer simulations, using the shapes of real asteroids.

In this kind of defense, a nuclear device would go off some distance from the asteroid, not on it.

The blast sends out a burst of X-rays that heats one side of the asteroid and turns part of its surface into vapor. That vapor rushes off into space, and the pressure it puts on the surface pushes the asteroid the other way.

The goal is to push the asteroid, not smash it. Breaking it apart could turn one big threat into smaller pieces that could still be deadly.

A nuclear blast is a different approach from crashing a spacecraft into an asteroid, which NASA’s DART mission tested in 2022.

Moore has worked on this question since a 2024 experiment at Sandia’s Z machine, a lab device that produces intense bursts of X-rays.

That experiment showed for the first time that X-rays could push a small piece of asteroid material.

Next, he wanted to know how a full-size asteroid would respond. Most researchers had treated asteroids as perfect spheres because that made the math easier, he said.

Real asteroids have irregular shapes that a perfect sphere cannot capture.

“You can make estimates that way, but asteroids come in all kinds of odd, lumpy shapes,” Moore said.

He found a way forward in a colleague’s work on how objects in space give off gas.

“I think we had an aha moment when we realized we could do this,” he said. “No more spheres. We would be able to model deflection for any asteroid.”

Moore built the new model by joining two computer programs that Sandia already used for very different jobs.

One usually simulates fast, high-energy events, such as experiments on the Z machine. The other usually handles weak forces that change slowly, like the drag the solar wind puts on a satellite.

In the new model, the first program works out how the X-rays heat the surface and turn part of it to gas.

The second follows that gas as it spreads across the asteroid’s real 3D shape, and it calculates the pressure on every part of the surface.

“The key innovation here was figuring out how to combine the two simulation approaches,” Moore said.

He also pointed to speed. “Our new algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough,” he said. “With the old models, computers just couldn’t handle it.”

To use the model, the team loads in an asteroid’s shape, which can come from detailed 3D images taken by passing spacecraft.

They then set the size of the blast, how far away it goes off, and which side it hits.

The program maps how much of each part of the surface turns to vapor. From that map, it works out how hard the asteroid gets pushed and how fast it spins afterward.

The team tested the model on three real asteroids with very different shapes. Bennu is the asteroid NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft sampled in 2020. The other two were Itokawa and Golevka.

For each one, the researchers tried blasts at close range and farther away. They also changed which way the asteroid was facing when the X-rays arrived.

In the simulations, orienting Bennu at its most favorable angle, instead of its worst, gave it up to nearly twice as much push.

The difference was larger for the other two, at up to nearly four times for Itokawa and five times for Golevka.

In one simulation, the blast changed an asteroid’s speed by about 0.15 inch (3.9 millimeters) per second from one angle. From another angle, it was only about 0.03 inch (0.8 millimeter) per second.

The asteroid and the blast were the same both times, and only the side facing the X-rays was different.

The aim also affected how fast an asteroid spun after the blast. For one asteroid, the change in its spin rate varied 17-fold depending on which side faced the blast.

“Our study shows how important it is to aim carefully,” Moore said. “Pick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day.”

To run the model, the team needs a fairly accurate picture of an asteroid’s shape from every side. In a real emergency, there might not be time to get one.

Placing a nuclear device at the right distance, on the right side of an asteroid speeding through space, would also be hard.

Another unknown is what happens to the whole asteroid.

“Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface,” he said. “We can’t predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet.”

When the researchers applied the blast pressures to a loose, Itokawa-like pile of boulders, the rock thrown off was lopsided, just like the vapor.

Predicting whether a whole asteroid breaks apart will take more research and better modeling tools. An X-ray blast would set off many effects at once, and those effects could change one another.

That full calculation is what Moore and other scientists are working toward.

The full study was published in the journal Icarus.

In the run-up to the COP31 U.N. climate change conference, scientists have revealed that global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to drop by 0.4% this year, driven by growth in installed wind and solar power capacity, as well as oil price hikes caused by the Iran conflict. But climate goals are still unlikely to be met.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The world's carbon emissions from oil, gas and coal are projected to decrease by 0.4% this year, driven partly by the expansion of solar and wind power capacity and the price increases caused by the Iran conflict, according to a new report.

The 2026 Global Carbon Budget report was published in the journal Earth System Science Data Nov. 10 and is due to be presented at the U.N. Climate Change Conference's COP31 meeting in Antalya, Turkey, this week.

Global carbon emissions have increased steadily since record-keeping began. This year is projected to have a slight decrease in fossil-fuel emissions, but that is partly due to price increases caused by the Iran conflict.

It is the first time annual carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels have fallen since the coronavirus pandemic in 2020. But the overall emissions picture suggests the world is still likely to miss key climate goals.

"It is an encouraging sign that the growth of emissions is slowing and decarbonisation efforts are starting to make a difference," said Joeri Rogelj, a climate scientist at the Centre for Environmental Policy at Imperial College London who wasn't involved in the research. "However, at 0.4%, the projected decline is very small," Rogelj told Live Science in an email.

The report projects 38.2 billion metric tons (42.1 billion U.S. tons) of emissions of the climate-warming greenhouse gas CO2 from fossil fuel sources this year. Greenhouse gases trap heat by absorbing the sun's radiation, and as their concentrations in the atmosphere increase, so do global average temperatures, leading to altered weather patterns and higher sea levels, as well as other major impacts.

The war with Iran has resulted in restricted fuel availability and high prices, with a corresponding reduction in demand

Part of the 0.4% reduction in CO2 emissions is attributable to 40 countries that have cut emissions over the past decade while growing their economies. These include the U.S., Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Japan and about 30 countries in the European Union, the researchers reported.

When it comes to some of the biggest emitters, annual CO2 emissions are projected to decrease by 0.9% in China, 1.3% in the U.S., 1.5% in the European Union and 1% in Japan, but India's annual CO2 emissions are projected to grow by 4.4%.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Carbon emissions are projected to decrease slightly in the U.S., China and the E.U. but to increase in India.

Fossil-fuel-linked CO2 emissions from the rest of the world are projected to decrease by 0.7%, driven mainly by a 1.9% drop in oil emissions. Some of the report authors suggested in an accompanying paper in Nature Climate Change that this is a short-term response to the global supply constraints and increased prices triggered by the Iran conflict.

"The war with Iran has resulted in restricted fuel availability and high prices, with a corresponding reduction in demand," Rogelj said.

While fossil fuel emissions and demand for oil are declining globally, overall demand for energy is actually increasing.

"Based only on the demand for energy, which has grown, we would have expected an increase in fossil CO2 emissions by about 0.8 gigatonnes," said study co-author Judith Hauck, a biogeoscientist at the Alfred Wegener Institute, Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research in Germany.

About two-thirds of that increase in demand is being met by solar and wind power and electric vehicles, showing that clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions, Hauck said. However, the hike in energy prices that resulted from the Iran conflict also decreased demand by 0.4%, she said.

"So only together with the energy crisis did we bring the change in emissions down to negative," Hauck told Live Science, adding that she expects CO2 emissions to rebound if the conflict ends, as they did after the temporary emissions drop caused by the lockdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The exceptional circumstances that energy markets experienced this year make it clear that the small projected emissions decline is no reason to declare that emissions are now reducing, but there are hopeful signs, Rogelj said.

"Despite my muted enthusiasm about whether these lower emissions for 2026 represent the start of a long-term decline, the analysis shows encouraging signs of deeper long-term structural changes," he said. "But this shift must accelerate to ensure it is not outpaced by energy demand growth."

The report found that clean energy growth isn't yet fast enough to drive a steady decline in global CO2 emissions attributable to fossil fuels. The study authors expect that to happen in the next few years, Hauck said, as long as there is a continued push to deploy solar and wind power, batteries and electric vehicles.

CO2 emissions from fossil fuels are just part of the picture, though. Because of increases in human-caused peat fires, deforestation and forest fires linked to dry El Niño conditions, total global CO2 emissions from all sources this year are projected to increase slightly from 42.8 billion metric tons (47.2 billion U.S. tons) last year to reach a record 43.3 billion metric tons (47.7 billion U.S. tons) this year, according to the report.

This means that the total budget of CO2 that can be emitted before global warming reaches 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels is now just 150 billion metric tons (165 billion U.S. tons) ‪—‬ equivalent to less than four years of emissions at the current rate.

Hauck, like many climate scientists, thinks we have already missed our chance to hit the 1.5 C target and could only get back to that level through extensive removal of CO2 from the atmosphere.

"I'm still hopeful for something between 1.5 and 2 C [3.6 F]," Hauck said. "But for 1.5 degrees, we would need to see such a drastic strong drop in emissions. Based on what we've seen in the past years, even with this strong increase in avoided emissions, I don't think we can make that."

To halt global warming from increasing ever further, the world needs to be more ambitious in its planned emissions cuts, said Rogeli. We need to bring annual emissions down to zero to protect future generations from a double whammy of “having to try to transform economies so that they produce less climate pollution, while dealing with the impacts and damages of an increasingly adverse climate system," he said.

Editor's Note: This article was updated on Wednesday, Nov. 11 at 8:45 a.m. E.D.T. to note that the conclusions about the effect of the Iran conflict on fossil fuel emissions came from a Nature Climate Change paper written by some of the report authors.

#6377. Archaeologists Found 2,500-Year-Old Battle Lines From a Conflict No One Knew Ever Happened

The Iron Age palisade likely blocked an invading army. But who built it—and who were they afraid of?

Archaeologists sifting through portions of Denmark’s western peninsula ahead of a highway expansion keep uncovering remnants of the area’s past, often in small snapshots: a grave here, an axe there, or maybe sometimes even the foundation of an ancient home. They certainly weren’t expecting to find the remains of battle lines in West Jutland, indicating a conflict they didn’t know ever transpired.

“The find came as a complete surprise to us,” Michael Alrø Jensen, curator at Museum Vest, said in a translated statement. “It points to previously unknown conflicts in West Jutland dating back to the earliest part of the Iron Age.”

The find showed up via a 2,500-year-old line of pits, which experts believe fighters created during the Iron Age to block hostile incursions along an ancient West Jutland thoroughfare. The discovery came as archaeologists from the museum examined fields along Route 11, between Varde and Korskro, before the Danish Road Directorate began a highway expansion.

Experts dubbed the battle lines, which were found beneath a field near Schaefergården, a “post-hole alignment,” likely from around 500 B.C.E. The lines feature a long series of closely spaced holes in which one end of pointed wooden posts were buried to form a defensive palisade.

“Our best theory is that there was a fear of an invading army arriving from the north via the ‘Drivvej’ route, and that attempts were therefore made to control and block the passage,” Jensen said.

More evidence may still lie buried at the site. Experts note that the current Route 11 alignment between Varde and Korskro matches the ancient “Drivvej,” or Drove Road, that was the main transportation line through West Jutland for centuries. The modern road project adds an additional lane to the two-lane highway and shows how closely the ancient road—whose origin date remains unknown—matches the modern setup.

Still, the find raises questions. Archaeologists and historians don’t know who developed the defensive structure—or why. The team hopes that additional work in the area may offer fresh clues about the ancient mystery.

Attempts to pinpoint answers to a 2,500-year-old question got a bit muddy as the excavations revealed artifacts from a range of eras in spots that hadn’t been searched previously. Archaeologists now have evidence of human activity along the road from the first Stone Age farmers, who buried their dead in small mounds through the Bronze Age, Iron Age, and into the Viking Age (including the discovery of a 4,500-year-old battle axe buried alongside a Stone Age warrior).

“What we are most excited about is that we have found traces from so many different periods within a relatively small area,” Jensen said. “We have suddenly gained a wealth of new pieces that provide much greater insight into how people lived and moved about in this region over several thousand years.”

Every new discovery provides nuance to the historical record, whether the remains of a house, farm, or grave. Museum Vest hopes to learn more by excavating additional burial mounds. The various discoveries in the region together form a narrative of humans’ transformation of the land, first into farming plots and then into villages. “Once our work is complete, we hope to be able to offer the local community a more cohesive narrative about the area they live in,” Jensen said.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6376. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

A 2019 astronaut photo shows the near-perfect cone of a highly active volcano poking its heavily scarred and partially snow-covered head above a thick bank of low-lying clouds over the Kuril Islands.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Atlasov Island, off the coast of Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula [50.84755357, 155.56126752]

What's in the photo? The summit of Alaid volcano peeking above a thick layer of low-lying clouds

Who took the photo? An unnamed astronaut on board the International Space Station

This eye-catching astronaut photo shows a towering, highly active Russian volcano poking its head above a thick bank of swirling clouds over the Kuril Islands.

The lofty peak is located on Atlasov Island, the northernmost of the Kuril Islands — a chain of roughly 50 largely uninhabited volcanic landmasses stretching along a fault line that runs between Russia and Japan in the Sea of Okhotsk. Altasov lies 40 miles (65 kilometers) off Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula, which is also renowned for its volcanic activity.

The island consists mainly of a single, massive volcano, called Alaid, which is known for its near-perfect cone shape. Alaid reaches up to 7,497 feet (2,285 meters) above sea level, making it the tallest peak in the Kuril Islands.

Alaid has erupted at least nine times in the past 50 years, including a major outburst in April 1981 that ejected a 1,250-mile-long (2,000 km) plume of thick smoke and ash into the atmosphere, according to the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program.

Its most recent eruption occurred between September and November 2022, when a river of lava flowed down its flank (see below). During this outburst, the volcano also spit out smoke and ash that was spotted from space alongside another eruption plume coming from the nearby island Paramushir.

Alaid last erupted in November 2022 and unleashed a scorching lava flow down its snow-covered slopes. This photo also shows what Atlasov Island looks like when it is not obscured by clouds.

In the astronaut's photo, roughly half of Atlasov Island rises above a deep, low-lying bank of swirling clouds. The summit of Alaid, crowned by a roughly mile-wide (1.6 km) caldera, is also obscured by clouds. (The volcano was not erupting when the photo was taken.)

Farther down the volcano's flanks are a series of snow-filled gullies carved out by lava flows from previous eruptions. Eagle-eyed viewers may also be able to spot some parasitic cones — small openings where lava burst through in the past — around the edge of the cloud layer, according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The area surrounding a cluster of parasitic cones on the volcano's northwest flank (top right in the photo) is devoid of vegetation ‪—‬ a result of another major eruption in 1972, which scoured the surrounding landscape with hot ash. A 2009 study revealed fresh signs of recovery in the affected area, but noted that it could take hundreds of years for vegetation to return to pre-eruption levels.

The clouds are not the only thing the island rises above. Alaid is essentially the summit of a much larger underwater volcano that lies beneath the Sea of Okhotsk. The rest of the island has grown around the exposed cone as lava flows have reached sea level and solidified. Millions of years ago, this larger volcano was likely connected to the Kamchatka Peninsula via a land bridge that has since been submerged.

In 1981, a major eruption caused Alaid to unleash a massive plume of smoke and ash that reached up to 1,250 miles long.

Astronauts and satellites have snapped several other stunning shots of intriguing landmasses nearby, including a quartet of end-to-end volcanoes on Simushir Island and a set of volcanic "nesting dolls" on Onekotan Island.

And in 2022, the Landsat 8 satellite also spotted the iconic summit of Mount Vesuvius peeking through a gap in the clouds over Italy, just like Alaid.

A 2024 astronaut photo shows the icy surface of Pangong Lake breaking apart in the lofty Tibetan Plateau. The point where the ice meets the water almost perfectly matches a disputed border between China and India.

A 2020 astronaut photo shows the unique structure of Ol Doinyo Lengai, an active stratovolcano in Tanzania that was recently adorned with a bright white "ash cone." The explosive peak produces a rare type of lava that is unusually cool but travels remarkably quickly.

A 2010 satellite photo shows the point where a small lake bisects the snowy rim of an ancient glacier on Canada's Baffin Island. The rippling, snow-rimmed structure is the last remaining fragment of a colossal ice sheet that once covered large parts of North America.

#6373. Plant roots have a clever way to tell good and bad fungi apart, even though they both give off the exact same molecules

Good and bad fungi release the exact same chemical signal but plant roots still know which one is dangerous

A fungus growing on a crop sounds like bad news, but not all fungi are harmful. Plants also rely on helpful fungi to take up nutrients through their roots.

Attackers and partners alike are built from the same material, a sugar chain called chitin. Fragments of it end up in the soil whenever a fungus grows or breaks down.

A new study shows how a receptor on legume roots sorts those fragments by length.

Receptors tightly grip long chitin chains, the kind that come with a fungal attack, and raise the alarm. Short ones, the kind that partner fungi shed, barely register.

Kira Gysel and Kasper Røjkjær Andersen of the Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics at Aarhus University in Denmark led the work.

Simon Boje Hansen and Henriette Rübsam are the first authors, with co-authors at the University of Copenhagen and the French research center CERMAV. The experiments were done in two small legumes used as laboratory models, not in crops.

In an interview with Earth.com, Gysel said the puzzle was that chitin looks the same along its whole length.

“It’s the same sugar repeated, like a string of identical beads, with nothing to tell one part of the chain from another,” she said.

Chitin is the main building block of a fungal cell wall. When a fungus grows or gets broken down, pieces of the chain of different lengths end up in the soil. Roots read these fragments of fungi to keep track of the microbes around them.

Long fragments usually come with an attack and, in legumes, they set off a much stronger defense than short ones. Short fragments come with the helpful fungi that plug into roots and exchange nutrients with the plant.

How a root told the two apart was the open question.

The team produced the outer part of a root receptor called CHIP13 and tested how hard it holds chitin chains of different lengths. It held an eight-sugar chain more than 1,000 times more tightly than a five-sugar chain.

Then they froze the receptor into crystals with the long chain attached and mapped it, atom by atom.

The receptor holds the chain at three points. Two are standard chitin-binding pockets found in related receptors. The third sits between them, and the team named it the bridge domain, because it spans the middle of the chain.

Gysel told Earth.com that the structure answered the question at a glance.

“CHIP13 holds the chain at three main contact points, and the central one, the bridge domain, is what coordinates binding of the long chitin chain,” Gysel said.

“Only chains long enough to reach all three are held tightly and can activate the plant’s immune response. It’s really a molecular measuring tape.”

Swapping out two amino acids near the bridge cut the receptor’s grip 100-fold. In a second legume, barrel medic, mutant plants given a version of the matching receptor with the same two swaps didn’t regain their response to chitin.

Legume roots also need a second receptor, CERK6, to respond to chitin, and CERK6 can barely hold chitin at all. Boje Hansen said that had been a puzzle.

“It turns out the two receptors split the work: one recognizes the signal, the other passes it on. Neither can do the job alone,” he said.

In leaf cells engineered to carry both receptors, CHIP13 pulled in CERK6 only once chitin was bound. The weakened version of CHIP13 didn’t recruit it at all.

The team’s model is a pair of CHIP13 receptors holding chitin and recruiting two CERK6 partners, which then pass the alarm into the cell.

To test the receptors in a living plant without altering its genes, the team raised nanobodies – tiny antibody-like proteins made by immunizing a llama – that plug each receptor’s chitin-binding site.

They soaked intact seedlings of the model legume Lotus japonicus in them. When asked by Earth.com what else about the research stood out, Gysel pointed to that experiment.

“We simply applied them to plants from the outside, and we weren’t sure it would work at all,” she said. “We thought the plant cell wall would block the nanobodies from reaching the receptors on the surface of the plant cells.”

The nanobodies reached the receptors. Seedlings treated with the CERK6 blocker responded to chitin about as weakly as plants missing that gene, and the CHIP13 blocker cut the response sharply too.

Both legumes are laboratory models, and the measuring tape hasn’t been checked in a crop. The bridge domain can be predicted in many related receptors across higher plants, but a predicted domain isn’t a tested one.

Gysel said the two receptors are only a glimpse of a larger immune system. Plants use many related receptors to monitor soil microbes. How those receptors work together, and whether others read signals by length, is what her group wants to find out next.

The stakes she described are agricultural. Strengthening the chitin alarm could make crops more resistant to fungal disease, but only if it doesn’t also fire at the fungi the roots depend on.

“Knowing how the long chitin chains are read helps us improve crops without tipping the balance, so we don’t weaken their defenses to make room for helpful fungi, or the other way around,” Gysel said.

Which crop receptors carry a bridge domain, and whether they measure chitin the same way, is the next thing to check.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

#6371. The Best Gooloo Portable Jump Starters Do More Than Just Bring an Engine Back to Life

The compact A3, value-packed A5, and heavy-duty A7 all punch above their weight in power capacity and air pressure, plus offer essentials like a flashlight and charging ports.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’re looking for a reliable portable jump starter, Gooloo is one of the first names that comes to mind. The brand has a reputation for offering models with impressive jump-starting power and capacity, which I’ve confirmed in my testing.

While Gooloo has plenty of portable jump starters in its lineup, three in particular are worth comparing for features relative to price point: the compact 3,000-amp A3, the value-packed 4,000-amp A5, and the heavy-duty 6,000-amp A7.

Along with at least double the amps required to jump most vehicles, large trucks, and SUVs, Gooloo’s devices stand out for more than the ability to bring an engine back to life. Many, including the models I mention above, double as tire inflators and include advanced functions, such as automatic modes for, say, automobile and bicycle tires, and auto shutoff when a user-set pressure is reached. They’re also packed with a variety of handy features, like flashlights and USB ports.

The 3,000-amp Gooloo A3 is the smallest and lightest of the three portable jump starters, but it’s mighty. The tire inflator has 1.24 cubic feet per minute (cfm) and 150 psi ratings that are impressive for the A3’s size, which means it can fill a 17-inch tire (common in most passenger vehicles) from 30 to 36 psi in under one minute. A 2.8-inch color screen simplifies stepping through five preset inflation modes: SUV, car, bike, ball, and custom.

Like the Gooloo units below, the jump starter has a boost button and 10 protection features, including for short-circuit (reversing the leads when connected to a battery) and overheating. There are various nozzles for inflating tires, sports equipment such as balls, and other items.

Features include a 30-watt USB-C input/output port, a USB-A output, an LED flashlight, and a USB-A to USB-C cable to charge its internal battery. For proper storage, there is a sturdy soft-sided carrying case. One downside: I found the air compressor louder than the other Gooloo units here and some of the other tire inflators I’ve tested.

The Gooloo A5 is a little larger and heavier; however, it ups the ante with 4,000 amps of peak power and 20,000 milliampere-hours (mAh) of capacity that can crank even the largest passenger vehicles and retain a charge for more than a year. The tire inflator is rated 160 psi, and Gooloo doesn’t provide a cfm spec but says the A5 can inflate a 15-inch car tire from 30 to 36 psi in 30 seconds. In my testing, it was noticeably faster and quieter than the A3. Like the A3, though, it has five automatic inflation modes, automatically stops when a preset inflation pressure is reached, and comes with five nozzles.

The A5’s 3.2-inch color display is my favorite of the three units. It’s easy to read, even in bright sunlight, and a big plus is its 45-watt USB-C charging cable. It’s attached at one corner so that you won’t lose it, plus it doubles as a carrying handle.

There’s also a USB-A output port for charging devices such as a phone or tablet, a three-mode flashlight, and a USB-A to USB-C charging cable that’s used to recharge the unit from 0 to 100 percent in about six hours. It also comes with a decent storage case.

The Gooloo A7 is larger and heavier than the A3 and A5, and I found it slightly more stable than the A3 and A5 thanks to its square footprint.

At 6,000 amps, it packs the most power and has 24,000 mAh of capacity so that it can crank larger engines and hold a charge longer. But at almost three times the price without an appreciable increase in power, the only way to justify its much higher cost is with the significantly robust tire inflator with a 5.30 cfm rating that’s more than double that of any of the portable tire inflators I’ve previously tested.

It’s also the only unit here that has a very powerful 12.4-cfm “blower” function that, along with a supplied hose and four adapters, can be used to quickly inflate and deflate large items such as a blow-up mattress or stand-up paddleboard.

As with the A3 and A5, it also has five inflation presets as well as automatic shutoff when the set inflation pressure is reached, a three-mode flashlight, and a boost button. It has a USB-C input/output for charging the device and powering other portable electronics, as well as a USB-A output port.

The 3.7-inch display is the largest of the three units, making it quickly readable at a glance, although the display isn’t as vibrant as the A5’s color display. It’s a disappointment that the device comes with a cheap nylon carrying bag instead of the sturdier cases provided with the A3 and A5. An appreciated perk, though, is a supplied set of lightweight work gloves to protect your hands and keep them from getting dirty while using the device to jump-start an engine or inflate a tire.

All three of these combination portable jump starters will get you out of a jam, and each has advantages and disadvantages. The A3 is a great choice for the majority of motorists. A friend of mine chose this device for his motorcycle because of its compact size. I recommend the A5 for its impressive capabilities compared to its price—and it has the best display. The higher cost of the A7 is only worth it if you own a larger vehicle or need the inflate-and-deflate blower function. But no matter which one you pick, you’ll be relieved you have it on hand the next time you’re stranded with a dead battery or deflated tire, or worse yet, both.

Other Portable Jump Starter Combos We Recommend

The Noco delivers an impressive 2,000 amps of peak power and has 16,000 mAh capacity, while the tire inflator pumps out 2.3 cfm and up to 100 psi. It has auto shutoff and memory settings like other air compressors I’ve tested but adds “dwell” technology that pauses and then resumes inflation when a set pressure is reached to ensure proper inflation. Its 60-watt USB-C port recharges the device from 0 to 100 percent in about an hour.

With 4,000 amps of peak current and 24,000 mAh of capacity, the Wolfbox can jump-start up to 10.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines. It holds a charge for more than a year. The 1.5-cfm air pump takes one minute to inflate a 17-inch tire from 30 to 36 psi. It also has a 65-watt USB-C in/out port to quickly recharge the internal battery, two USB-A ports to charge other devices and includes a 400-lumen, three-mode LED flashlight.

With 1,200 amps, this device cranks up to 6.0-liter gas and 3.0-liter diesel engines. Spark and reverse-polarity protection won’t send current to the battery clamps unless they’re securely and correctly connected. A built-in pump provides 140 psi and comes with adapters for bikes, balls, and other items. Included are a USB-C charging cable and port, a USB-A outlet, a clamshell carrying case, and lifetime customer service.
